statement: HUD's latest worst case needs report attributes the elevated needs to wage growth too weak to make rent affordable for low-income renters and to sustained rental demand, which it ties to record immigration.
anchor:
This year’s report shows two realities. The first is that economic growth has been insufficient to
lift the wages of low-income renting families high enough to make rent affordable. The second is
that national macroeconomic policies, such as record immigration, have combined to drive
sustained high rental demand, which has continued to place upward pressure on rent prices.
context: Published July 2025, during the second Trump administration. The report's immigration section rests on research it summarizes on immigration and metropolitan rents; its footnote lists Camarota (1998), Edo (2015), Mussa et al. (2017), Myers et al. (2006), Orrenius and Zavodny (2007) and Saiz (2007), the last a peer-reviewed study of immigration and rents. The report's own decomposition (EV-HOU-029) attributes 321,000 added cases to household formation, which it describes as largely driven by immigration and declining marriage, but does not measure immigration on its own. Its counts come from HUD tabulations of the American Housing Survey and are treated as data (EV-HOU-020 to 024); this causal reading needs independent research before the dossier relies on it.

statement: HUD's 2024 homelessness report names several likely causes of the record count: the affordable housing crisis, inflation, stagnating wages, systemic racism, public health crises, natural disasters, immigration, and the end of pandemic-era prevention programs including the expanded child tax credit.
anchor:
Our worsening national affordable housing crisis, rising inflation, stagnating wages among
middle- and lower-income households, and the persisting effects of systemic racism have stretched
homelessness services systems to their limits. Additional public health crises, natural disasters that
displaced people from their homes, rising numbers of people immigrating to the U.S., and the end to
homelessness prevention programs put in place during the COVID-19 pandemic, including the end of the
expanded child tax credit, have exacerbated this already stressed system.
context: Published December 2024 under the Biden administration. The list of factors is the report's interpretation, offered without estimates of how much each contributed.

statement: HUD's decomposition of the 2021-2023 change in worst case needs: household formation (4.73 million new households), which the report describes as largely driven by record immigration and a long-term decline in marriage rates, added an estimated 321,000 cases, the largest upward demographic factor; a shift toward homeownership removed 247,000, rising renter incomes 163,000 and a narrower rental assistance gap 169,000, so the four demographic factors together reduced needs by 258,000; a tight rental market added 196,000.
anchor:
Household Formation. The nation added 4.73 million households between 2021 and 2023,
explaining a proportional increase of 321,000 cases of worst case needs.
2023, so an improved rental assistance gap accounts for 169,000 fewer cases of worst case needs.

factors indicates that the demographic factors affecting the number of unassisted VLI renter
households were sufficient to reduce worst case needs by 258,000 cases, but the inability of the
tight rental market to meet the demand largely offset that decrease by contributing 196,000 cases.
Of the four demographic factors, national household formation, largely driven by record levels of
immigration and a continued long-term decline in marriage rates, would have been expected to
increase worst case needs by 321,000 cases. A shift from renting to homeownership diminished
that effect by an estimated 247,000 cases. Improvement in renter incomes accounted for a further
reduction of 163,000 cases.
context: The report's quantified analysis (a shift-share decomposition of American Housing Survey estimates). It folds immigration into household formation together with declining marriage rates and does not estimate immigration's share on its own. Household formation is the largest upward demographic factor; homeownership, incomes and assistance more than offset it. So the analysis is consistent with immigration adding to needs, without measuring how much.

statement: Across U.S. metropolitan areas, an immigration inflow equal to 1% of a city's population is associated with increases of about 1% in average rents and housing values, an effect an order of magnitude bigger than in labor markets.
anchor: Immigration pushes up rents and housing values in US destination cities.

An immigration inflow equal to 1% of a city’s population is associated with increases in average rents and housing values of about 1%. The results suggest an economic impact that is an order of magnitude bigger than that found in labor markets.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Urban Economics, 2007), Wharton author, no advocacy affiliation; the estimate that analysts on every side cite. It measures metro-level effects of legal immigration over the 1980s and 1990s, before supply has time to respond fully.

statement: The 1980 Mariel boatlift added 9% to Miami's renter population; Miami rents rose 8% to 11% more than in comparison cities between 1979 and 1981 and were still 7% higher by 1983. Higher-quality units were not affected, and units occupied by low-income Hispanic residents saw an extra 8% rise.
anchor: This exogenous immigration shock added an extra 9% to Miami’s renter population in 1980. I find that rents increased from 8% to 11% more in Miami than in the comparison groups between 1979 and 1981. By 1983 the rent differential was still 7%.

Rental units of higher quality were not affected by the immigration shock. Units occupied by low-income Hispanic residents in 1979 experienced an extra 8% differential hike with respect to other low-income units. Relative housing prices moved in the opposite direction from rents in the short run.
context: Peer-reviewed natural experiment (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2003). A sudden low-income inflow into one city, which shows the effect at the bottom of the market but not how a national inflow spreads. EV-HOU-050 is by the same author, so it is not counted as independent.

statement: Within metropolitan areas, housing values grew more slowly in neighborhoods where immigrants settled: a neighborhood whose foreign-born share went from 0 to 30 percent would have values about 6 percent lower. The authors attribute this more to demand for segregation by race and education than to foreignness itself.
anchor: Within metropolitan areas, we find that housing values have grown relatively more slowly in neighborhoods of immigrant settlement.
in an area where the share of the foreign born changes from 0 to 30 percent, housing values can be expected to be about 6 percent lower.
these results may be driven more by the demand for residential segregation based on race and education than by foreignness per se.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2011). Shows that metro-wide increases can coexist with local declines as some natives move out. Shares an author with EV-HOU-050, so no independent corroboration yet.

statement: During the recent immigration boom, unauthorized immigrant worker inflows equal to 1% of a local area's employment raised local house prices 2.2% and rents 1.4%, without expanding housing supply. For the average local market that explains about 30% of house-price growth and 20% of rent growth over the boom; for the median metropolitan area the implied effects, 2.9% on prices and 1.9% on rents, are relatively modest.
anchor: an increase in unauthorized immigrant worker flows equal to 1% of a local area’s initial employment increased local house prices by 2.2% and increased local rents by 1.4%.
A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that UIWF can explain about 30% of the total growth in house prices and 20% of total growth in rents over the boom period for the average local market.

yields implied effects of UIWF on house prices and rents of 2.9% and 1.9%, respectively. These effects amount to relatively modest contributions to the median MSA’s total increases in house prices and rents over this period.
These inflows also raised local house prices and rents without expanding housing supply
context: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas working paper (March 2026) by Federal Reserve System economists using administrative microdata; not yet peer-reviewed. HUD and administration officials have cited it as confirming that illegal immigration raised housing costs. It covers the same years as HUD's decomposition (EV-HOU-029), and it finds effects concentrated where migrants settled.

statement: The post-pandemic surge of about 6.5 million migrants who entered outside usual legal pathways raised natives' rents by 1.6% and natives' wages by 0.9%. Declines in domestic in-migration almost wholly offset the surge in the average metropolitan area, and the rent effect apparently turned negative in 2023-2024 (-1.4%, imprecisely estimated).
anchor: an unprecedented inflow of about 6.5 million migrants who entered outside of usual legal pathways.

it raised U.S. natives’ wages 0.9% over the period. The surge left native employment rates unaffected, but increased natives’ rent by 1.6%. Declines in net domestic in-migration almost wholly offset the surge migration in the average metro
The effect on rents apparently became negative in 2023-2024, though this -1.4% is imprecisely estimated.
context: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference draft (September 2026) by Rutgers, Dallas Fed and University of North Florida economists; may change before publication.

statement: Foreign-born householders accounted for 25 percent of household growth from 2019 to 2023, amid particularly strong native-born household growth. After immigration ramped up in 2022, house price and rent growth slowed, and by 2023 rent growth had stalled while the surge continued. Immigrants were 34 percent of construction trades workers in 2023, against 18 percent of the whole workforce.
anchor: Foreign-born householders accounted for 25 percent of household growth from 2019–2023 amid particularly strong native-born household growth

After immigration ramped up in 2022, growth rates of house prices and rents slowed substantially. By 2023, as the surge in immigration continued, home price growth fell even further while rent growth completely stalled.
Immigrants accounted for 34 percent of those who worked in construction trades in 2023, far higher than their 18 percent share of the overall workforce
context: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies blog (October 2024); a university center funded partly by housing-industry and foundation sponsors. The timing argument contests HUD's reading that household formation was largely driven by immigration (EV-HOU-029).

statement: The staggered rollout of the Secure Communities enforcement program brought large and persistent reductions in construction workforce and homebuilding: three years in, the average treated county permitted 2,578 fewer housing units, saw 1,994 fewer new homes, paid 18% more for new construction, and saw average home prices up 10%.
anchor: Treated counties experience large and persistent reductions in construction workforce, residential homebuilding, and increases in home prices.
2,578 fewer housing units are permitted, and 1,994 fewer newly constructed homes enter the market.
Three years after SC implementation, the average new construction parcel is 18% more expensive relative to the baseline
we find that average home prices increase by 10% by the 3nd year after implementation.
context: Academic working paper (October 2024), not yet peer-reviewed. Cato's analyst notes the rollout was probably not random. The supply side of immigration: enforcement raised prices through lost construction labor.

statement: The Congressional Research Service notes that immigration raises housing demand but also construction labor supply, so it is generally not posited as one of the main drivers of higher housing costs. It cites an Urban Institute estimate that deporting undocumented construction workers could reduce the construction workforce by 1.7-1.8 million.
anchor:
generally immigration is not posited as one of the main
drivers of increased housing costs given that the supply effects, at least partially, balance out the
demand effects.

the Urban Institute estimated
that deportations of undocumented construction workers could result in a decrease of 1.7-1.8
context: Nonpartisan legislative-branch agency, April 2026.

statement: The UK's Migration Advisory Committee, reviewing international studies, finds most credible estimates put the effect of a one-percentage-point rise in the immigrant share at 0 to 3% on house prices, with smaller rent effects (mean estimate 0.87%, median 0.64%). Applied to the UK, immigration would account for around 4-6% of the rise in house prices since the mid-1990s.
anchor: most credible estimates suggest that a one-percentage-point increase in the immigrant share of the population increases house prices by between 0 and 3%. Rent effects are typically slightly smaller.
mean estimate of 0.87% and the median estimate at 0.64%.
immigration would therefore account for around 4-6% of the total increase in house prices since the mid-1990s
context: Independent public body advising the UK Home Office (June 2026). International synthesis; UK supply conditions differ from U.S. ones.

statement: The Center for Immigration Studies reports that immigrant-headed households rose 2.4 million after January 2021, perhaps 1.4 million of them from illegal immigration, and that a 5-point higher recent-immigrant share in a metro area goes with a 12 percent higher rent relative to income for U.S.-born households, a figure it calls only a simple correlation.
anchor: since January of 2021 the number of immigrant-headed households is up 2.4 million, with perhaps 1.4 million of this increase due to illegal immigration.
a 5-percentage point increase in the recent immigrant share of a metro area’s population is associated with a 12 percent increase in the average U.S.-born household’s rent, relative to their income.
Of course, this is only a simple correlation and does not include homeowners.
locator: summary, Housing; Immigration and Rent Affordability section
context: Written testimony to a House subcommittee (September 2024) by a think tank that favors lower immigration. The rent figure is an uncontrolled correlation.

statement: The Cato Institute's immigration analyst, who favors more immigration, agrees that immigrants increase house prices, by a factor of 3 to 10 more than they affect wages, and notes that about 30 percent of construction workers are immigrants, so deporting them would reduce the growth in housing supply.
anchor: Vance is correct in saying that immigrants increase the price of houses.
Relative to the labor market, the marginal immigrant affects housing prices by a factor of 3 to 10 more than wages, depending on your preferred wage elasticity.
about 30 percent of all construction workers are immigrants
Deporting those workers or halting more immigrants will reduce the growth in the housing supply.
context: Libertarian think tank blog (October 2024); commentary on existing research, not new estimates.

statement: The Economic Policy Institute argues that higher housing costs are caused not by immigration but by housing markets failing to meet new demand with new homes, pointing to the large run-up in home prices in 2020 and 2021 just as immigration was plummeting, and warns that mass deportation could raise housing costs by shrinking the construction workforce.
anchor: Increased housing costs are caused not by immigration, but by the failure of U.S. housing markets to meet any new demand with more housing units rather than higher prices
This can be seen most clearly in the very large run-up in home prices in 2020 and 2021, just as rates of immigration were plummeting.

Anti-immigrant reforms (like mass deportations) done in the name of preserving housing affordability for U.S.-born workers could well see large increases in housing costs due to resulting shortages of workers employed in residential construction.
context: Progressive, labor-aligned think tank (October 2024); advocacy synthesis, not new estimates.

statement: The number of people in U.S. homeless shelters rose an unprecedented 43 percent between 2022 and 2024. Asylum seekers accounted for about 60 percent of that rise, concentrated in New York City (77,352 increase), Chicago (14,590), Massachusetts (13,353) and metropolitan Denver (6,556); the data suggest little connection between asylum seekers and the rise in unsheltered homelessness.
anchor: an unprecedented 43 percent increase in the number of people residing in homeless shelters in the United States between 2022 and 2024
we estimate that asylum seekers accounted for about 60 percent of the two-year rise in sheltered homelessness during this period
New York City (77,352 increase), Chicago (14,590 increase), Massachusetts (13,353 increase), and metropolitan Denver (6,556 increase).
the data suggest little connection between asylum seekers and the 2022-2024 increase in unsheltered homelessness.
context: University of Chicago working paper (April 2025), also NBER Working Paper 33655; the lead author's poverty-measurement work is cited across parties. Places with a right to shelter housed arriving asylum seekers in shelters, which raised shelter counts.

statement: Where house prices are above the cost of building, the housing market is not functioning well and housing is too expensive for all households in that market, not just poorer ones. But Glaeser and Gyourko conclude that the vast majority of U.S. homes are priced near or below their full social costs of replication.
anchor: But if housing prices are above this cost in a given area, then the housing market is not functioning well—and housing is too expensive for all households in the market, not just for poorer ones.
Thus, our conclusion that the vast majority of homes are priced near or below their full social costs of replication is robust to virtually any assumption we could make.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2018); Harvard and Wharton authors who favor deregulation; quoted from NBER Working Paper 23833.

statement: Using data from U.S. metropolitan areas from 1980 to 2016, Federal Reserve Board researchers find sizeable effects of supply constraints on house prices but modest-to-negligible effects on rents, housing consumption, location choice and housing expenditures.
anchor:
We find sizeable effects of supply constraints on house
prices, but modest‐to‐negligible effects on rent, lot size, structure consumption, location choice
within metropolitan areas, sorting across metropolitan areas, and housing expenditures.

data from
US metropolitan areas from 1980 to 2016
context: Federal Reserve Board working paper (FEDS 2020-044) by two Board economists and an academic; later published in the Journal of Urban Economics. A counterweight to accounts that put renter burden mainly down to regulation.

statement: CRS finds national supply indicators mixed: homes per person and per household have been fairly steady since 1980, but vacancy rates are below the 1980-2024 average, so supply is more constrained than before. Higher interest rates raise the cost of financing construction, though the link to construction is not always strong; population-adjusted starts in 2025 were down roughly 27% for single-family homes, 76% for condominiums and 7% for rental apartments.
anchor:
The total number of homes per person and the total number of homes per household
have been fairly steady since 1980, indicating similar supply conditions over this period.

Vacancy rates are currently lower than the 1980-2024 average, indicating that supply is currently more
constrained than previously.

Higher interest rates
increase the costs of financing residential construction and renovation.

although the relationship between interest rates and construction is not always strong
or linear.

starts in 2025 were down by roughly 27% for single-family units, 76% for
multifamily for sale units (i.e., condominiums), and 7% for multifamily for rent units
context: Nonpartisan legislative-branch agency (April 2026). The low vacancy supports the "tight rental market" in HUD's decomposition (EV-HOU-029).

statement: Rents rose 8.3 percent over the 12 months to December 2022, and rent growth eased to 3.8 percent over the 12 months to May 2025. Governor Kugler credits the moderation partly to more multifamily construction; lower-end rents cooled less, in part because new construction was aimed at the high end.
anchor: Rents surged early in the pandemic recovery, rising 8.3 percent over the 12 months ending in December 2022. This year, rent growth eased to 3.8 percent over the 12 months ending in May.

The recent increase in multifamily construction has contributed to this moderation. For lower-end properties, we have not seen as much of a cooling in rental inflation, in part because new construction has been aimed at the high end of the market.
context: Speech by a Federal Reserve Board governor appointed by President Biden (July 17, 2025), drawing on Board staff research.

statement: Governor Kugler summarizes research as finding that rent growth increases in the short run after a wave of immigration but may not persist if supply expands to meet demand, and notes that the share of renters spending more than 30 percent of income on rent was about 40 percent in both 2019 and 2023.
anchor: Academic research examining immigration flows finds that rent growth increases in the short run after a wave of immigration, but these rent increases may not persist if the housing supply expands over time to meet the increase in housing demand.
The share of renters spending more than 30 percent of their income on rent was about the same in 2023 as it was in 2019, about 40 percent in both years.
context: As EV-HOU-066. At the median, rents did not outrun incomes from 2019 to 2023, so the strain is concentrated among lower-income renters.
note: also causes/kugler2025 quote 2

statement: By early 2026 an influx of new multifamily supply had contained rent increases: the share of newly completed units leased within three months hit a record low of 45 percent in the second quarter of 2025, and the rental vacancy rate reached 7.4 percent in February 2026, the highest since that series began in 2017.
anchor: In particular, an influx of new multifamily housing supply has contained rent increases, as seen in Figure 2 below.
After reaching a record low of 45 percent in the second quarter of 2025, the latest reading of 46 percent in the third quarter has shown little improvement.
The most recent reading of 7.4 percent in February 2026 was the highest since the series began in 2017
locator: para. 2; absorption rate section; vacancy section
context: Richmond Fed economist's blog (2026), views the author's own; vacancy from Apartment List. The tight market of 2021-2023 has since loosened.

statement: The shift to remote work explains over one-half of the 18.9 percent increase in U.S. real house prices from 2019 to 2023; each additional point of remote work raised house prices 0.92 percent and also raised rents, through demand for more space at home.
anchor: We show that the shift to remote work explains over one-half of the 18.9 percent increase in U.S. real house prices from 2019 to 2023.

we estimate that an additional percentage point of remote work causes a 0.92 percent increase in house prices after controlling for spillovers from migration. This finding reflects an increase in demand for home space: remote work causes an increase in residential rents
context: NBER working paper (2022, revised May 2025) by a San Francisco Fed economist and a UC San Diego economist; a demand driver unrelated to immigration.

statement: Federal Reserve Board staff find that quality-adjusted rent growth differed little across the income distribution from 1985 to 2019: cumulatively, rent rose 81 percent for the top income fifth and 72 percent for the bottom fifth.
anchor: how quality-adjusted changes in rent have differed for households across the income distribution from 1985 to 2019.
We find that rent growth differentials across groups were fairly minor overall.
Cumulating over the entire period, rent increased by 81 percent at the top quintile, and by 72 percent at the bottom quintile.
context: FEDS Notes (November 2021), Board staff. So rising burden at the bottom reflects incomes more than faster rent inflation for the poor; covers the years before 2020 only.

statement: The median renter household spent about 18 percent of income on rent in 1960 and 29 percent at the time of writing; renters in the bottom fifth went from about 47 to 63 percent. Rents largely tracked incomes until the Great Recession; after 2007 incomes fell while rents rebounded, a trend the authors attribute at least in part to stagnant real incomes for renters.
anchor: The median renter household in 1960 spent about 18 percent of their income on rent; today they spend 29 percent. Renters who were in the bottom fifth of the income distribution devoted about 47 percent of their income to rent in 1960, compared to 63 percent today.
Over this period, rents largely tracked income until the Great Recession. Since 2007, incomes have plummeted while rents have rebounded after a brief dip.
This trend is at least in part due to stagnant real incomes for renters over this period
context: Peer-reviewed volume chapter (NBER Working Paper 21071; University of Chicago Press, 2016) by NYU and University of Chicago economists.

statement: Over four decades there is little evidence that owner-occupied housing became less affordable, and the median renter devoted modestly more income to housing, but rent burdens for poor households rose sharply.
anchor: There is little evidence that owner-occupied housing has become less affordable. In contrast, there have been modest increases in the fraction of income that the median renter household devotes to housing. We find pronounced increases in the rent burdens for poor households.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2004), UC Berkeley economists; weighs income distribution, housing quality and regulation as causes.

statement: Under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, child poverty more than doubled from 5.2 percent in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022, a return to pre-pandemic levels: the 2022 rate was not statistically different from 2019's 12.6 percent.
anchor:
SPM rates more than doubled for
children (individuals under the age
of 18) in 2022, increasing 7.2 percentage points, from 5.2 percent
in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022.
This represents a return to prepandemic SPM child poverty levels, as
the 2022 rate was not statistically
different from the 2019 rate (12.6
percent)
note: Census measurement; P60 reports for later years exist and should be added in the next refresh.

statement: The Census Bureau attributes the 2022 rise in Supplemental Poverty Measure rates in part to the expiration of the expanded refundable tax credits and stimulus payments.
anchor:
driven in part by the expiration of
the expanded refundable tax credits and stimulus payments.
context: The statistical agency's own reading of its measure; the measure counts tax credits as income, so the link follows from its construction.

statement: Using 943,568 Household Pulse responses from April 2021 to May 2022, monthly child tax credit payments reduced food insufficiency among families with children by at least 2.4 percentage points (19%), while the lump-sum payment reduced the share behind on housing payments by at least 1.2 percentage points (10%).
anchor: We produce difference-in-difference estimates to identify how monthly and lump-sum CTC payments affected food and housing hardship among a sample of 943,568 respondents between April 2021–May 2022.

The monthly CTC payments reduced food insufficiency among families with children by at least 2.4 percentage points (19%), but the lump-sum payment did not reduce food insufficiency. Instead, the lump-sum payment reduced the likelihood that families with children were behind on housing payments by at least 1.2 percentage points (10%).
context: Columbia Center on Poverty and Social Policy working paper (September 2022) by authors who supported the expanded credit; later published in AEA Papers and Proceedings (not opened). The housing effect is modest.

statement: Landlords filed over one million eviction cases in 2024 in the jurisdictions Eviction Lab tracks, roughly four percent fewer than in a typical pre-pandemic year, but over six percent above the historical average without New York City, where filings were at 52% of their pre-pandemic level. 15 of 35 cities had higher filing rates than before the pandemic; in Phoenix the rate rose from 10.6% to 14.3%.
anchor: Landlords filed over one million eviction cases in 2024 in the jurisdictions we track. That’s a small drop relative to 2023 and roughly four percent fewer eviction cases filed than in a typical pre-pandemic year
If we remove New York—the city with the largest renter population of the country—eviction filings were over six percent above historical average.
Of the 35 cities in the ETS, 15 had a higher eviction filing rate in 2024 than was typical before the pandemic.
Phoenix experienced the second largest jump in its filing rate, from 10.6% prior to the pandemic to 14.3% in 2024.
Filings in New York City are at 52% of their pre-pandemic level
locator: paragraph 3; section on city trends; conclusion
context: Court-record counts from about a third of U.S. renter households; the Lab supports tenant protections.

statement: Landlords filed 1.23 million eviction cases in 2025 at the sites Eviction Lab monitors, slightly fewer than the 1.26 million of 2024 and 3.2% below the post-pandemic average; the average filing rate was 8.0%, and only 5% in New York City. Black renters were 28% of renters but 39% of those named in filings.
anchor: Across all sites that we currently monitor, landlords filed 1.23 million eviction cases in 2025. This total was slightly lower than in 2024 (1.26 million cases) and marks the second year in a row of declining eviction filings (see Figure 1). Overall, eviction case filings in 2025 were 3.2% below the post-pandemic average.
Across all the locations we track, the average eviction filing rate was 8.0%
Despite making up 28% of the renter population, we estimate that 39% of eviction filings in 2025 named a Black defendant.
the eviction filing rate in NYC was only 5% in 2025.
locator: About our eviction tracking system; pull quote; race section; filing-rate section
context: As EV-HOU-076.

statement: While the CDC eviction moratorium was in force, from September 4, 2020 to July 31, 2021, tracked sites saw 47.2% of the eviction filings of a typical year, and the filing rate fell from about 8.1% to around 3.8%. Eviction Lab estimates the moratorium helped prevent 1.55 million filings nationwide.
anchor: Between September 4, 2020 and July 31, 2021, we observed 368,398 eviction filings across the jurisdictions we monitor. This represents less than half as many eviction filings (47.2%) as we would expect over the same period in a typical year.
Normally, the eviction filing rate in the areas we monitor is about 8.1% over this time period. With the CDC eviction moratorium in place, that fell to around 3.8%.
We estimate that the CDC moratorium helped to prevent 1.55 million eviction filings nationwide.
context: The national figure is an extrapolation from tracked sites, not a count.

statement: Colburn and Aldern test common beliefs about what drives homelessness in a city (mental illness, drug use, poverty, weather, generosity of public assistance and low-income mobility) and find that none explains the regional variation across the country; housing market conditions, the cost and availability of rental housing, offer a far more convincing account.
anchor: test a range of conventional beliefs about what drives the prevalence of homelessness in a given city—including mental illness, drug use, poverty, weather, generosity of public assistance, and low-income mobility—and find that none explain the regional variation observed across the country.
Instead, housing market conditions, such as the cost and availability of rental housing, offer a far more convincing account.
context: Book (University of California Press, 2022) by a University of Washington academic and a data scientist; quoted from the publisher's description.

statement: A model of homeless counts in the 25 largest U.S. metropolitan areas finds the relationship between homelessness and rental costs strongest in New York, Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and Seattle, and that the inferred rise in homelessness from 2011-2016 depends on prior beliefs about how accurate the counts are.
anchor: To examine trends in homeless population counts in the 25 largest U.S. metropolitan areas, we develop a dynamic Bayesian hierarchical model for time-varying homeless count data.

evidence is presented that the inferred increase in the rate of homelessness from 2011-2016 depends on prior beliefs about the accuracy of homeless counts. A main finding of the study is that the relationship between homelessness and rental costs is strongest in New York, Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and Seattle.
context: Peer-reviewed (Annals of Applied Statistics, 2019); academic statisticians.

statement: The Council of Economic Advisers estimated that deregulating housing in the 11 metropolitan areas with significantly supply-constrained markets would cut overall U.S. homelessness by 13 percent, and by 31 percent on average in those areas (54 percent in San Francisco, 40 percent in Los Angeles). It also argued that more shelter, as a substitute for permanent housing, increases homelessness, and named the tolerability of sleeping on the street and individual characteristics that make homelessness more likely as further drivers.
anchor:
We estimate that if the
11 metropolitan areas with significantly supply-constrained housing markets were
deregulated, overall homelessness in the United States would fall by 13 percent.

would fall by much larger amounts in these 11 large metropolitan areas, for example by 54
percent in San Francisco, by 40 percent in Los Angeles, and by 23 percent in New York City. On
average, homelessness would fall by 31 percent in these 11 metropolitan areas

A larger supply of substitutes to permanent housing through shelter provision also increases
homelessness.

(ii) the tolerability of sleeping on the street (outside of shelter or housing); (iii) the supply of
homeless shelters; and (iv) the characteristics of individuals in a community that make
homelessness more likely.
context: Published September 2019 under the first Trump administration; critical of Housing First. Agrees that housing costs are central but places the cause in regulation and adds shelter policy and climate.

statement: Cold places uniformly have low rates of unsheltered homelessness, while warm places display wide variation.
anchor: They find that cold places uniformly have low rates of unsheltered homelessness, while warm places display wide variation.
context: AEI working paper (conservative think tank); later in the Journal of Housing Economics. Climate shapes whether homeless people are unsheltered, a factor HUD does not list. Corinth served on the Council of Economic Advisers in 2019, so EV-HOU-081 is not counted as independent of it.

statement: Across U.S. communities, one additional permanent housing bed was associated with 0.12 fewer homeless people on the streets and in shelters, an association fully muted after the first year; the homelessness rate was significantly associated with median rent.
anchor: one additional permanent housing bed is associated with 0.12 fewer homeless people on the streets and in shelters; however, this negative association is fully muted after the first year.
The homelessness rate is significantly associated with median rent
context: AEI working paper; the author later served on President Trump's Council of Economic Advisers. A peer-reviewed version appeared in the Journal of Housing Economics (not opened).

statement: Only 5.3 million (1 in 4) eligible renter households receive federal rental assistance; worst case needs rose 32 percent from 2007 to 2019 while assisted households rose 3 percent. Nearly 6 in 10 low-income cost-burdened Black renters have extremely low incomes, against less than half of White renters, and White renters make up a smaller share of assisted households than of those in need.
anchor: Only 5.3 million (1 in 4) eligible renter households receive federal rental assistance due to funding limitations.

From 2007 to 2019, the number of renter households with very low incomes either paying more than half their income for rent or living in severely substandard housing, known as worst-case housing needs, increased 32 percent. During this same period, the number of households receiving federal rental assistance rose only 3 percent.
Nearly 6 in 10 low-income cost-burdened Black renters have extremely low incomes, compared to less than half of white renters.
White renters make up a smaller share of assisted households compared to those in need of assistance.
context: Progressive think tank that advocates more rental assistance (2022), using HUD tabulations. Its account of why Black renters are more often assisted is deeper poverty plus programs that admit the poorest first.

statement: In the pandemic Emergency Rental Assistance program, Black renters' share of recipients was 21-22 percentage points higher than their share of eligible renters, and extremely low-income renters were 64% of recipients, twice their share of the eligible; the evaluators note that this matters because income distributions vary by race and ethnicity.
anchor: Extremely low income renters were overrepresented: at 64%, their share of the recipient population was twice their share of the eligible population.
Black renters were strongly overrepresented among recipients of ERA – their share of the recipient population was 21-22 percentage points higher than their share of the eligible population.
This matters for the representation of ethnic and racial groups, because income distributions vary by race and ethnicity.
context: Federal evaluation unit (GSA Office of Evaluation Sciences, 2023) with Treasury data. A different program from HUD's, so it bears on HUD's reading by analogy.

statement: The Family Options Study randomly assigned 2,282 families in homeless shelters across 12 sites. Priority access to long-term rent subsidies reduced homelessness and food insecurity and improved other aspects of adult and child well-being, at a cost 9 percent higher than usual care; the other interventions had little effect. The subsidy reduced the share of family heads with any employment from 57.5 percent to 52.0 percent but had no effect on average earnings.
anchor: The Family Options Study randomly assigned 2,282 families recruited in homeless shelters across 12 sites to priority access to one of three active interventions or to usual care in their communities.

priority access to long-term rent subsidies reduced homelessness and food insecurity and improved other aspects of adult and child well-being relative to usual care, at a cost 9 percent higher. The other interventions had little effect.

reduced the proportion of family heads with any employment during this period (a one-year period approximately centered on the 37-month follow-up point) from 57.5 percent to 52.0 percent but had no effect on average earnings
locator: abstract; footnote on National Directory of New Hires data
context: Randomized trial funded by HUD and run by Abt Associates with academic co-authors (Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 2018). HUD commissioned it under the Bush administration and published its main reports under the Obama administration (2015-16); the journal article is the academic authors'. The long-term subsidies were mostly Housing Choice Vouchers.

statement: In the same trial, families given priority access to short-term rent subsidies (rapid re-housing) or transitional housing did no better on average than families in usual care; short-term subsidies led to comparable results at a 9 percent lower cost.
anchor: Although on average families given priority access to short-term rent subsidies and transitional housing did no better than families assigned to usual care
The third option studied, short-term rent subsidies, led to comparable results to usual care at a 9 percent lower cost.
context: As EV-HOU-086.

statement: In Chicago's randomized voucher waiting-list lottery, using a voucher reduced labor force participation by around 4 percentage points (6 percent) and quarterly earnings by $329 (10 percent), and increased TANF participation by around 2 percentage points (15 percent); the authors find no evidence that housing-specific mechanisms such as neighborhood quality promote work.
anchor: housing voucher use reduces labor force participation by around 4 percentage points (6 percent) and quarterly earnings by $329 (10 percent), and increases Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program participation by around 2 percentage points (15 percent).
We find no evidence that the housing-specific mechanisms hypothesized to promote work, such as neighborhood quality or residential stability, are important empirically.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Review, 2012).

statement: Ten to 15 years after families were randomly offered Moving to Opportunity vouchers, the program improved adults' physical and mental health but had no detectable effect on economic outcomes or youth schooling, with mixed results by gender on other youth outcomes.
anchor: We show that ten to 15 years after baseline, MTO: (i) improves adult physical and mental health; (ii) has no detectable effect on economic outcomes or youth schooling or physical health; and (iii) has mixed results by gender on other youth outcomes
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Review, 2013).

statement: Children whose families used a Moving to Opportunity voucher to move to a lower-poverty area before age 13 had annual incomes $3,477 (31%) higher in their mid-twenties than the control group mean of $11,270; the same moves had, if anything, negative effects on children over 13.
anchor: children whose families take up an experimental voucher to move to a lower-poverty area when they are less than 13 years old have an annual income that is $3,477 (31%) higher on average relative to a mean of $11,270 in the control group in their mid-twenties.
the same moves have, if anything, negative long-term impacts on children who are more than 13 years old when their families move
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Review, 2016); quoted from NBER Working Paper 21156. Katz co-authored EV-HOU-089, and Chetty and Hendren EV-HOU-091, so those are not counted as independent.

statement: In Seattle and King County, search assistance, landlord engagement and short-term financial help raised the share of voucher families moving to high-upward-mobility areas from 15 to 53 percent, driven primarily by customized search assistance; barriers in the housing search significantly increase segregation by income.
anchor: The treatment increased the fraction moving to high-upward-mobility areas from 15 to 53 percent. A second trial reveals this treatment effect is driven primarily by customized search assistance.
barriers in housing search significantly increase residential segregation by income
context: Peer-reviewed randomized trials (American Economic Review, 2024) with two housing authorities.

statement: Records for about 85,000 new voucher recipients a year in 433 metropolitan housing authorities from 2015 to 2019 show that 61% leased a home within six months; lease-up was significantly lower in metro areas with fewer vacancies, more spatial variation in rents and older housing.
anchor: administrative data from about 85,000 voucher recipients (annually), in 433 U.S. metropolitan housing authorities, between 2015 and 2019.
We estimate that 61% of voucher recipients successfully leased a home within six months of receiving their vouchers during the five years of our study, 2015 to 2019.
In metro areas with fewer housing vacancies, more spatial variation in rent prices, and an older housing stock, lease-up rates are significantly lower.
context: Summary (Institute for Research on Poverty, 2024) of NYU Furman Center researchers' peer-reviewed study.

statement: In paired tests of landlords in five metropolitan areas, the denial rate for voucher holders was 78 percent in Fort Worth, 76 percent in Los Angeles and 67 percent in Philadelphia, but 31 percent in Newark and 15 percent in Washington, D.C., the two sites where source-of-income laws require landlords to accept vouchers.
anchor:
Denial
rates were highest in Fort Worth (78 percent) and
Los Angeles (76 percent) and only somewhat
lower in Philadelphia (67 percent). Rates were
substantially lower in Newark (31 percent)
and Washington, D.C. (15 percent).

In three of the five
sites, the landlord denial rate was 67 percent or higher. In the two sites with lower levels of
landlord denial (less than 31 percent), source-of-income antidiscrimination laws require landlords
to accept vouchers.
context: Published by HUD's research office in 2018, under the first Trump administration. Paired-testing study for HUD by the Urban Institute (2018), a center-left research organization; a pilot in five sites.

statement: Source-of-income anti-discrimination laws had mixed effects on where voucher holders live: substantively important reductions in neighborhood poverty and small but significant reductions in minority concentration.
anchor: This research found that the impacts of SOI laws on locational outcomes are mixed. We found substantively important reductions in neighborhood poverty rates associated with the implementation of SOI laws and small but statistically significant reductions in minority concentration as well.
context: Peer-reviewed (Housing Studies, 2014).

statement: Making vouchers more generous across a whole metro area mainly benefits landlords through higher rents, with minimal effect on neighborhood and unit quality; indexing rent ceilings to neighborhood rents leads voucher holders to move to neighborhoods with lower crime, poverty and unemployment.
anchor: A policy that makes vouchers more generous across a metro area benefits landlords through increased rents, with minimal impact on neighborhood and unit quality. A second policy that indexes rent ceilings to neighborhood rents leads voucher holders to move into higher quality neighborhoods with lower crime, poverty, and unemployment.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2018). The second policy is what HUD calls Small Area Fair Market Rents.

statement: An increase in vouchers did not raise the overall price of rental housing; the largest price increases were for units near the maximum allowable voucher rent in cities with inelastic housing supply.
anchor: We do not find that an increase in vouchers affected the overall price of rental housing but do estimate differences in effects based on an individual unit's rent before the voucher expansion.
the largest price increases were for units near the maximum allowable voucher rent in cities with an inelastic housing supply.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2015).

statement: CBPP finds federal rental assistance sharply reduces homelessness and other hardship and lifts 3 million people out of poverty, citing a study in which it cut the share of families in shelters or on the street by three-fourths; 60 percent of non-disabled working-age assisted households include a worker.
anchor: Federal rental assistance sharply reduces homelessness and other hardship and lifts 3 million people out of poverty.
One study found that rental assistance reduced the share of families living in shelters or on the street by three-fourths
among non-disabled, working-age households with rental assistance, 60 percent include at least one worker and the majority receive assistance for less than three years.
context: Progressive think tank that advocates more rental assistance (2019).

statement: In a New York trial, two hundred twenty-five homeless people with mental illness were randomly assigned to housing contingent on treatment and sobriety or to immediate housing without prerequisites. The immediate-housing group got housed earlier and stayed stably housed; the control group used more substance abuse treatment, but substance use and psychiatric symptoms did not differ.
anchor: Two hundred twenty-five participants were randomly assigned to receive housing contingent on treatment and sobriety (control) or to receive immediate housing without treatment prerequisites (experimental).

The experimental group obtained housing earlier, remained stably housed, and reported higher perceived choice. Utilization of substance abuse treatment was significantly higher for the control group, but no differences were found in substance use or psychiatric symptoms.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Journal of Public Health, 2004); the lead author founded Pathways to Housing, the program tested.

statement: In Canada's multi-city At Home/Chez Soi trial of 950 people with serious mental illness, Housing First participants spent 71% of the time in stable housing against 29% under usual treatment; differences in other outcomes narrowed by the end of the second year.
anchor: A sample of 950 participants with serious mental illness
Housing First participants spent more time in stable housing than participants in treatment as usual (71% versus 29%, adjusted absolute difference [AAD]=42%, p<.01).
differences between the two groups were attenuated by the end of the second year.
context: Peer-reviewed (Psychiatric Services, 2016); funded by the Mental Health Commission of Canada; Tsemberis is a co-author.

statement: A meta-analysis of four randomized trials, all at high risk of bias, found Housing First participants more likely to be housed at 18-24 months (risk ratio 2.46) and with fewer emergency department visits (rate ratio 0.63), with no clear difference in substance use and imprecise effects on most short-term health outcomes.
anchor: were more likely to be housed at 18–24 months (risk ratio=2.46; 95% CI 1.58 to 3.84).
Intervention groups experienced fewer emergency department visits (incidence rate ratio (IRR)=0.63; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.82)

We included four studies, all with ‘high’ risk of bias. The impact of HF on most short-term health outcomes was imprecisely estimated, with varying effect directions. No clear difference in substance use was seen.
context: Peer-reviewed systematic review (Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, 2019), University of Glasgow.

statement: A CDC Community Guide review of twenty-six U.S. and Canadian studies found that, compared with treatment-first programs, Housing First decreased homelessness by 88% and improved housing stability by 41%.
anchor: Twenty-six studies in U.S. and Canada met inclusion criteria. Compared with Treatment First, Housing First programs decreased homelessness by 88%, improved housing stability by 41%.
context: Peer-reviewed systematic review for the Community Preventive Services Task Force (2020), an independent panel that the CDC supports; published under the first Trump administration.

statement: The median Housing First cost was $16,479 per person per year in U.S. studies, against median benefits of $18,247; the benefit-to-cost ratio was 1.80:1 for U.S. studies and 1.06:1 including Canadian ones. The authors conclude that economic benefits exceed the cost of Housing First programs in the U.S., and that there were too few studies to judge cost-benefit in Canada.
anchor: The median intervention cost per person per year for U.S. studies was $16,479 and for all studies, including those for Canada, it was $16,336. The median total benefit for the U.S. studies was $18,247 per person per year
The benefit-to-cost ratio for U.S. studies was 1.80:1, and for all studies including those for Canada it was 1.06:1.
The evidence from this review shows economic benefits exceed the cost of Housing First programs in the U.S. There were too few studies to determine cost–benefit in the Canadian context.
context: Peer-reviewed economic review for the CDC Community Guide (2022, Biden administration). The 1.80:1 summarizes the studies' own ratios, which is why it differs from the ratio of the median cost and median benefit. Shares an author with EV-HOU-101.

statement: Linking At Home/Chez Soi participants to health records, mortality did not differ between Housing First and usual care (pooled adjusted hazard ratio 0.83, 95% confidence interval 0.43-1.22).
anchor: Mortality rates were not different in the HF compared with TAU groups (pooled log mortality rate ratio, −0.07; 95% CI, −0.36 to 0.22). The pooled adjusted hazard ratio comparing mortality in the HF and TAU groups was 0.83 (95% CI, 0.43-1.22).
context: Peer-reviewed (JAMA Network Open, 2025), trial investigators.

statement: The Congressional Research Service concludes that permanent supportive housing helps increase days spent in housing and reduce days spent homeless, while reductions in service use and costs, substance use and mental health improvements are less clear and may require more than a move out of homelessness.
anchor:
Overall, based on a review of the research, PSH
helps increase days spent in housing and reduce days spent homeless, showing that PSH can be a
successful way to end homelessness. The outcomes in other areas are not as clear

reductions in service use and costs, reductions in substance use, and mental health
improvements may depend on individual needs and circumstances and require more than a
successful move out of homelessness.
context: Nonpartisan legislative-branch agency.

statement: Housing First reports document excellent housing retention, but data on homeless clients with active and severe addiction are limited, so policymakers should be cautious about generalizing the results to them.
anchor: Housing First reports document excellent housing retention, despite the limited amount of data pertaining to homeless clients with active and severe addiction.
policymakers should be cautious about generalizing the results of available Housing First studies to persons with active addiction when they enter housing programs.
context: Peer-reviewed review (Milbank Quarterly, 2009) by VA and University of Alabama researchers.

statement: A Manhattan Institute critic argues that proponents overstate Housing First's ability to end homelessness, its cost-effectiveness and its ability to improve lives, and that it has been shown effective for individuals but not in ending homelessness at the community level.
anchor: proponents overstate the ability of Housing First to end homelessness, the policy’s cost-effectiveness, and its ability to improve the lives of the homeless.
Housing First has not been shown to be effective in ending homelessness at the community level, but rather, only for individuals.
context: Conservative think tank (2020).

statement: A July 2025 executive order directs federal agencies toward ending support for "housing first" policies, and directs HUD to take steps to require recipients of federal housing and homelessness assistance to increase requirements that participants with substance use disorder or serious mental illness use treatment or mental health services as a condition of participation.
anchor: ending support for “housing first” policies that deprioritize accountability and fail to promote treatment, recovery, and self-sufficiency

(b) The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development shall, as appropriate, take steps to require recipients of Federal housing and homelessness assistance to increase requirements that persons participating in the recipients’ programs who suffer from substance use disorder or serious mental illness use substance abuse treatment or mental health services as a condition of participation.
context: Second Trump administration policy. The directives are primary law (an executive order); its reasons are recorded separately as analysis (EV-HOU-173).

statement: The July 2025 executive order calls past federal and state homelessness spending failed programs that address homelessness but not its root causes, and says "housing first" policies deprioritize accountability and fail to promote treatment, recovery and self-sufficiency.
anchor: The Federal Government and the States have spent tens of billions of dollars on failed programs that address homelessness but not its root causes
ending support for “housing first” policies that deprioritize accountability and fail to promote treatment, recovery, and self-sufficiency
context: Second Trump administration (executive order, July 2025). The administration's reading, not research. The order makes no claim about housing stability. On treatment and recovery outcomes the trial evidence is consistent with its doubts (EV-HOU-100, 105), and a conservative critic shares its view (EV-HOU-106). As that administration's analysis, it never carries a recommendation on its own.

statement: In Chicago from 2010 to 2012 (n = 4448), callers to a homelessness prevention line when emergency funds happened to be available were 76% less likely to enter a homeless shelter; averting a case of homelessness cost about $10,300 per person, and would cost much less with better targeting of benefits to lower-income callers.
anchor: Using data from Chicago from 2010 to 2012 (n = 4448), we demonstrate that the volatile nature of funding availability leads to good-as-random variation
those calling when funding is available are 76% less likely to enter a homeless shelter. The per-person cost of averting homelessness through financial assistance is estimated as $10,300
The per-person cost of averting homelessness through financial assistance is estimated as $10,300 and would be much less with better targeting of benefits to lower-income callers.
context: Peer-reviewed (Science, 2016); funding availability gives good-as-random variation.

statement: In a randomized trial in Santa Clara County, households offered emergency financial assistance (about $2,000 on average) were 81 percent less likely to become homeless within six months and 73 percent less likely within 12 months; the authors estimate $2.47 in benefits per net dollar.
anchor: the average treatment household received about $2,000 to pay rent, utilities and other housing-related expenses.
people offered the emergency financial assistance were 81 percent less likely to become homeless within six months of enrollment and 73 percent less likely within 12 months.
communities get $2.47 back in benefits per net dollar spent on emergency financial assistance.
context: Interview with the authors in The MIT Press Reader (2023), bylined Brian A. Jacob; the journal article (Review of Economics and Statistics) was not opened. Sullivan co-authored EV-HOU-108, so that is not counted as independent.

statement: In a randomized trial of New York City's Homebase prevention program among 295 families with children, treated families spent 22.6 fewer nights in shelter (9.6 against 32.2), and the share spending at least one night in shelter fell from 14.5% to 8.0%.
anchor: the analysis includes only the 295 families with at least one child
with the treatment group families spending on average 22.6 fewer nights in shelter (9.6 versus 32.2 nights) than the control group families (p=.03; see Table 2).
it reduced the percentage of families who spent at least one night in shelter from 14.5% to 8.0% and the percentage who applied for shelter from 18.2% to 9.3%.
context: Randomized evaluation by Abt Associates for the city agency that runs Homebase (2013).

statement: Across New York City, Homebase's rollout reduced family shelter entries by about 5% with census tracts weighted equally and 11% with community districts weighted equally.
anchor: The (geometric) average decrease in shelter entries was about 5% when census tracts are weighted equally, and 11% when community districts (which are much larger) are weighted equally.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Housing Economics, 2016); funded in part by the city agency. Effects across a whole city are smaller than for the households served.

statement: CRS reports that studies of LIHTC crowd-out range from little to nearly 100% of units replacing housing that would otherwise have been built, that studies typically find tenant subsidies more cost-effective than production subsidies, and that investor oversight ends 15 years after a property is awarded credits.
anchor:
The findings range from little crowding out to nearly 100%,
and depend on the market examined, the data used, and the
methodological approach of the researchers.

They typically
have found tenant subsidies to be more cost effective, but
the degree to which this is true depends on the specific
market.

investor oversight ends 15 years after a
property is awarded tax credits because investors are no
longer under the threat of losing or repaying credits.
context: Nonpartisan legislative-branch agency.

statement: Before the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), LIHTC cost the government an average of $14.4 billion a year; starting in 2026 the act permanently increases state allocation authority by 12% and lowered the 50% tax-exempt bond financing requirement to 25%. A project qualifies with at least 20% of units for households at or below 50% of area median income, or 40% at or below 60%; a third option lets 40% of units average no more than 60%, with no tenant above 80%, so some units can serve lower incomes.
anchor: Prior to enactment of P.L. 119-21, the LIHTC program was estimated to cost the government an average of $14.4 billion

Starting in 2026, the act permanently increases states’ annual allocation
authority by 12% and lowers the 50% tax-exempt bond financing requirement to 25%.

at least 20% of the units must be occupied by individuals with income of 50% or less of
the area’s median gross income (AMI)

at least
40% of the units must be occupied by individuals with income of 60% or less of AMI

the income test is satisfied if at least 40% of the units are occupied by tenants with an average
income of no greater than 60% of AMI, and no individual tenant has an income exceeding 80% of
AMI.
context: CRS summary of the law and cost estimates (July 2025).

statement: Government-financed units raise the total number of units in a market, but on average one subsidized unit adds only one-third to one-half of a unit to the housing stock; tenant-based vouchers seem more effective than project-based programs at reaching people who would otherwise lack their own housing.
anchor: We find that government-financed units raise the total number of units in a market, although on average one government-subsidized unit adds only one-third to one-half of a unit to the total housing stock.

Tenant-based housing programs, such as Section 8 Certificates and Vouchers, seem to be more effective than project-based programs at targeting subsidized housing units to people who otherwise would not have their own.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Public Economics, 2005).

statement: LIHTC accounts for one-third of recent multifamily rental construction, and the most robust estimates indicate that nearly 100% of LIHTC development is offset by fewer newly built unsubsidized rental units, though the confidence band allows smaller effects.
anchor: accounting for one-third of all recent multi-family rental construction

Our most robust IV estimates indicate that nearly 100% of LIHTC development is offset by a reduction in the number of newly built unsubsidized rental units, although the confidence band around this point estimate allows for less dramatic assessments.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Public Economics, 2010).

statement: Where projects get 30% higher tax credits, tracts receive about six more low-income units on a base of seven. LIHTC units crowd out nearby new rental construction in gentrifying areas but not in stable or declining areas, where they raise property values.
anchor: Tracts where projects are awarded 30% higher tax credits receive approximately six more low income housing units on a base of seven units per tract.
LIHTC units significantly crowd out nearby new rental construction in gentrifying areas but do not displace new construction in stable or declining areas.
raise property values in declining areas and reduce incomes in gentrifying areas
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Public Economics, 2009).

statement: LIHTC development in low-income neighborhoods raises nearby house prices 6.5%, lowers crime and attracts racially and income-diverse residents; in higher-income areas it causes house price declines of 2.5% and attracts lower-income households.
anchor: LIHTC development revitalizes low-income neighborhoods, increasing house prices 6.5%, lowering crime rates, and attracting racially and income diverse populations.
LIHTC development in higher income areas causes house price declines of 2.5% and attracts lower income households.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Political Economy, 2019); figures from the authors' 2017 working paper.

statement: In tenant data from state housing finance agencies, more than forty percent of LIHTC tenants had extremely low incomes, and the overwhelming majority of them also received rental assistance: 46 percent of all LIHTC households received some rental assistance, and 31 percent of those without it also had extremely low incomes.
anchor: We find that more than forty percent of tenants have extremely low incomes, and the overwhelming majority of such tenants also receive some form of rental assistance.
While 46 percent of all LIHTC households receive some form of rental assistance, only 29 percent of initial certifications have rental assistance.
a full 31 percent of LIHTC households not receiving rental assistance also have extremely low incomes
context: NYU Furman Center draft (2012), later in Housing Policy Debate. LIHTC reaches the poorest renters mainly when vouchers are layered on.

statement: Of roughly 2.5 million active LIHTC units, whose affordability requirements last at least 30 years, about one-third are set to expire by 2035, rising to roughly 40% once early exits are counted.
anchor: The NHPD shows that there were roughly 2.5 million active LIHTC units placed in service in 2022 or earlier
LIHTC affordability requirements last for 30 years at a minimum.
Without accounting for early exits, roughly one-third of all currently active LIHTC units are set to expire by 2035
we find that the number of units set to expire by 2035 increases to roughly 40%.
locator: Importance of LIHTC, by the numbers; introduction; key results
context: Chicago Fed community development staff (2025), from the National Housing Preservation Database.

statement: Housing authorities may not exceed their 1999 count of public housing units (the Faircloth limit). The stock fell from about 1.3 million units in 1993 to just under 920,000 in 2023; repair needs are estimated at $30 billion-$70 billion, against capital grants of $2 billion-$3 billion a year, and up to 455,000 units may convert under the Rental Assistance Demonstration, about 200,000 by November 2023.
anchor:
PHAs are prohibited from increasing their number of public
housing units above the total they had in 1999

In 1993, there were
approximately 1.3 million units of public housing; in 2023,
there were just under 920,000 units

estimates range from $30 billion-$70
billion in needed repairs. At the same time, annual funding
for public housing capital fund grants is generally in the
range of $2 billion-$3 billion.

Current law authorizes the conversion of
up to 455,000 public housing units under RAD; as of
November 2023, approximately 200,000 units had been
converted.
context: CRS summary of HUD data.

statement: Chicago children displaced by public housing demolitions, who mostly moved with vouchers, were 9 percent (4 percentage points) more likely to be employed as adults, earned $602 (16 percent) more a year, and had 14 percent fewer arrests for violent crimes than peers in buildings not demolished.
anchor: Displaced children are 9 percent (4 percentage points) more likely to be employed as adults relative to their non-displaced peers. Further, displaced children have $602 in higher annual earnings: an increase of 16 percent relative to their non-displaced counterparts.
displaced children have 14 percent fewer arrests for violent crimes in the years following demolition.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Review, 2018).

statement: HOPE VI redevelopment returned few original residents: in one tracking study, 19 percent lived in a revitalized development, 29 percent in other public housing, 33 percent rented with vouchers and 18 percent had left assisted housing, while grantees had expected 46 percent to return. Voucher users moved to tracts with much lower poverty, from 61 to 27 percent on average.
anchor: The Tracking Study found that 19 percent of the households surveyed were living in a revitalized HOPE VI development, 29 percent were living in other public housing properties, 33 percent were renting units using housing vouchers, and 18 percent had left assisted housing altogether.
on average, grantees expected 46 percent of residents to return.
the average census tract poverty rate for those who received vouchers dropped from 61 to 27 percent.
context: Urban Institute and Brookings review (2004) of HUD-funded studies.

statement: Auckland upzoned about three quarters of its residential land in 2016; an estimated 21,808 additional dwellings were permitted over the following five years, about 4.11% of the region's dwelling stock.
anchor: In 2016, the city upzoned approximately three quarters of its residential land to facilitate construction of more intensive housing.

This approach implies that 21,808 additional dwellings were permitted over the ﬁve years following the zoning reform, corresponding to approximately 4.11% of the dwelling stock of the Auckland region.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Urban Economics, 2023). A city-wide upzoning in a country with national planning law.

statement: After Chicago's 2013 and 2015 transit-area upzonings, there was no perceptible rise in new housing permits in upzoned areas over five years, while property values rose roughly in line with the added allowed density.
anchor: Implemented in 2013 and 2015, these changes were undertaken broadly, without specific association with new developments or other changes.
I found no perceptible uptick in new housing-unit permitting in the upzoned areas compared to the unaffected areas over five years.
I found an increase in property values in upzoned areas roughly equivalent to the increase in allowed density.
context: Peer-reviewed (Urban Affairs Review, 2020); quoted from the author's summary. Parcel-scale upzoning can raise land values before it raises building.

statement: From 2017 to 2022 Minneapolis increased its housing stock by 12% while rents grew 1%, against 4% and 14% in the rest of Minnesota; 87% of new units were in buildings of 20 or more units and just 1% in buildings of two to four units.
anchor: From 2017 to 2022, Minneapolis increased its housing stock by 12% while rents grew by just 1%. Over the same period, the rest of Minnesota added only 4% to its housing stock while rents went up by 14%.
Pew estimates that 87% were in buildings with 20 or more units, and just 1% were in buildings with two to four units.
context: Pew's housing initiative advocates zoning reform; a descriptive comparison, not a causal design. Most growth came from larger buildings, not the triplex rule.

statement: Five years after Minneapolis ended single-family-only zoning, home prices were 16-34% and rents 17.5-34% lower than in a synthetic counterfactual Minneapolis, but the effects are not the result of new housing supply; they are likely due to weakened demand.
anchor: home prices were 16–34% lower and rents 17.5–34% lower than a counterfactual Minneapolis.
The effects are consistent across multiple robustness exercises and are not the result of new housing supply, but are likely due to weakened housing demand.
context: Working paper (2025), Middlebury College economists; the post-2020 drop in demand in Minneapolis confounds the reform.

statement: In 1998 Houston cut the minimum lot size inside the I-610 Loop from 5,000 to 3,500 square feet, allowing even smaller lots (averaging 1,400 square feet) under conditions, and in 2013 extended the reform citywide; nearly 80,000 houses have been built on such small lots.
anchor: In 1998, they reduced the by-right minimum lot size from 5,000 to 3,500 square feet within the city’s I-610 Loop and permitted even smaller lots (down to an average of 1,400 square feet) for subdivisions that meet certain conditions. Then, in 2013, they extended the reform to cover all the land in the city with wastewater collection services.
In Houston, nearly 80,000 houses have been built on small lots made possible by minimum lot size requirements.
context: Mercatus Center (market-oriented, supports deregulation), 2023.

statement: The number of accessory dwelling units permitted each year in California grew from 1,336 in 2016 to 30,354 in 2024, a 20-fold increase; in 2024 ADUs were more than 26.6 percent of all homes permitted statewide.
anchor: Between 2016-2024, the number of ADUs permitted annually in the state grew from 1,336 to 30,354, a 20-fold increase. In 2024, ADUs comprised more than 26.6 percent of all homes permitted statewide.
context: State agency data from local annual progress reports. The state loosened local ADU rules over these years, but these are raw counts with no counterfactual; permits, not completions; rents of the units are not measured.

statement: Portland permitted over 1,400 accessory and middle-housing units in single-dwelling zones between August 1, 2021 and June 30, 2024; new middle-housing units sold for about $250,000 to $300,000 less than new detached houses in 2023-24, mostly because they are smaller.
anchor: Middle housing production has accelerated, with the City permitting over 1,400 ADU and middle housing units between August 1, 2021 and June 30, 2024 in single-dwelling zones.
In 2023-24, the average sales price of a new market-rate middle housing unit was about $250,000 to $300,000 less than that of a new market-rate single detached house, mostly due to size difference.
context: Self-evaluation by the bureau that wrote the policy (2025).

statement: In Helsinki, new market-rate housing triggers moving chains that quickly reach middle- and low-income neighborhoods: for each 100 new, centrally located units, roughly 31 vacancies open in the bottom fifth of neighborhoods by income and 66 in the bottom half.
anchor:
The supply of new market rate units triggers moving
chains that quickly reach middle- and low-income neighborhoods and individuals.
for each 100 new, centrally located market-rate units, roughly 31 (66) units are created in the bottomquintile (bottom half) of neighborhood income distribution through vacancies.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Urban Economics, 2023), Finnish register data.

statement: Chains of moves from new U.S. market-rate buildings quickly reach units in below-median-income neighborhoods, nearly 40 percent of the sixth round; a new building housing 100 people ultimately leads 45 to 70 people to move out of below-median-income neighborhoods, mostly within three years.
anchor: The sequence quickly reaches units in below-median income neighborhoods, which account for nearly 40 percent of the sixth round
Constructing a new market-rate building that houses 100 people ultimately leads 45 to 70 people to move out of below-median income neighborhoods, with most of the effect occurring within three years.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Urban Economics, 2023), Upjohn Institute.

statement: New large apartment buildings in low-income areas decrease rents in nearby units by about 6% relative to units slightly farther away, and increase in-migration from low-income areas; any amenity effect is not large enough to raise rents.
anchor: New buildings decrease rents in nearby units by about 6% relative to units slightly farther away or near sites developed later, and they increase in-migration from low-income areas.
If buildings improve nearby amenities, the effect is not large enough to increase rents.
context: Peer-reviewed (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2023).

statement: In New York City, within 500 feet of new high-rises, every 10% increase in the housing stock lowers rents by 1%, and every 10% increase in the condo stock lowers condo prices by 0.9%; the supply effect dominates the amenity effect.
anchor: I provide event study evidence that within 500 ft, for every 10% increase in the housing stock, rents decrease by 1%; and for every 10% increase in the condo stock, condo sales prices decrease by 0.9%.
I find that the supply effect dominates the amenity effect, causing net reductions in the rents and sales prices of nearby residential properties.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Economic Geography, 2022).

statement: In San Francisco, rents and displacement fall near new market-rate projects (rents by $22.77 - $43.18 a month, roughly 1.2 - 2.3%, within 500m; displacement risk by 17.14%), while parcels within 100m are 2.5 percentage points (29.5%) more likely to gentrify; affordable housing projects had no such spillovers.
anchor: I find that rents and displacement fall differentially near new market rate projects, while gentrification increases. In contrast, affordable housing does not have spillover effects.
monthly rents fall by $22.77 - $43.18 relative to trend, roughly 1.2 - 2.3%, for people living within 500m of a new project.
an additional project reduces displacement risk by 17.14% for people living within 500m.
Parcels within 100m of new market rate construction are 2.5 percentage points (29.5%) more likely to gentrify
context: Working paper (2021) using building fires to vary where projects are built; supported in part by the San Francisco Planning Department.

statement: In Minneapolis, comparing units within 300 meters of new construction with units 300 to 800 meters away, lower-priced rentals near new construction had 6.6 percent higher rents, while higher-priced rentals had 3.2 percent lower rents.
anchor: compare rent trajectories of units within 300 meters of new construction to a comparison group 300 to 800 meters away.

lower-priced rental housing close to new construction had 6.6 percent higher rents compared to the comparison group. New construction had the opposite effect on higher-priced housing; rents were 3.2 percent lower close to new construction.
context: Working paper (2020), University of Minnesota, funded in part by an affordable-housing advocacy group. A contrary finding for the low-priced submarket.
