statement: San Francisco's rent control expansion increased renters' probability of staying at their addresses by nearly 20%, but landlords treated by rent control reduced rental housing supply by 15%, causing a 5.1% city-wide rent increase; the substitution toward condos and high-end new rentals likely fueled the city's gentrification.
anchor: we find rent control increased renters’ probabilities of staying at their addresses by nearly 20%. Landlords treated by rent control reduced rental housing supply by 15%, causing a 5.1% city-wide rent increase.
This substitution toward owner occupied and high-end new construction rental housing likely fueled the gentrification of San Francisco
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Review, 2019); quoted from NBER Working Paper 24181.

statement: A Lincoln Institute paper finds no evidence that weakening an inclusionary policy lowered rents of high-cost units. It reports earlier studies finding inclusionary policies raised single-family prices by about 2 to 3 percent, and one finding permits declined 10 to 30 percent in the seven years after adoption.
anchor: This analysis fails to find evidence that weakening an inclusionary policy is associated with a decrease in the rental price of high-cost housing units.
find that inclusionary housing policies had a positive effect on the price of single-family houses, increasing prices by about 2 to 3 percent.
On average, they find that in cities with inclusionary housing policies permits declined 10 to 30 percent in the seven years after the policies were adopted.
context: Lincoln Institute working paper, not peer-reviewed; the Institute is generally favorable to inclusionary housing. Evidence on inclusionary zoning is mixed.

statement: When institutional single-family landlords merged, rents rose in neighborhoods where both firms owned homes, relative to other neighborhoods, while crime fell significantly there.
anchor: we show that rents increase in neighborhoods where both merging firms owned properties (i.e., overlapped neighborhoods) relative to other nonoverlapped neighborhoods. Meanwhile, the crime rate also significantly decreases in overlapped neighborhoods after mergers.
context: Peer-reviewed (Review of Financial Studies, 2023). Evidence of local market power, with a service gain.

statement: Institutional investors are concentrated in markets with lower housing values and higher shares of Black and non-college residents; they raise rents at 60% higher rates than the average increase when first acquiring a property; investor entry is not associated with gentrification.
anchor: We find that investor share is higher in markets with lower housing values and higher shares of black and noncollege residents, but higher median income.
investors raise rents at 60% higher rates than the average increase when first acquiring the property
We do not find evidence that investor entry is associated with gentrification
context: Philadelphia Fed working paper (2024); correlational.

statement: Growth of single-family rental REITs modestly raises prices and increases overall housing supply, with individual ownership rising at a similar rate; the authors conclude institutional landlords have had a limited impact on access to homeownership.
anchor: we find that SF-REIT growth modestly raises prices and increases overall housing supply, with individual ownership rising at a similar rate.
Overall, institutional landlords have had a limited impact on access to homeownership.
context: Philadelphia Fed working paper (2025).

statement: Montgomery County's Housing Production Fund, with $100 million of bonding capacity, can finance up to 6,000 new homes over 20 years, 1,800 of them affordable in perpetuity to renters earning 50 to 65 percent of area median income; construction loans are repaid when buildings move to permanent financing, so the money revolves.
anchor: With its $100 million bonding capacity, the HPF can finance up to 6,000 new housing units over 20 years, of which 1,800 will be affordable in perpetuity to renters earning between 50 and 65 percent of the area median income.

After construction is completed and units are leased, the initial bond financing is rolled over to permanent financing, paying back the principal balance to the HPF and unlocking those dollars to finance additional construction loans.
context: Urban Institute description (2024) of a prize-winning local model; projections, not an evaluation. No independent evaluation was found.

statement: More than two million U.S. households have an eviction case filed against them each year. Using random assignment of cases to judges, an eviction order increases homelessness and hospital visits and reduces earnings, durable goods consumption and access to credit in the first two years, and in the longer run raises debt and lowers credit scores.
anchor: More than two million U.S. households have an eviction case filed against them each year.

We find that an eviction order increases homelessness and hospital visits and reduces earnings, durable goods consumption, and access to credit in the first two years. Effects on housing and labor market outcomes are driven by impacts for female and Black tenants. In the longer-run, eviction increases indebtedness and reduces credit scores.
context: Peer-reviewed (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2024); quoted from the NBER working paper abstract.

statement: In a randomized trial in a Massachusetts District Court, about two-thirds of tenants offered full representation kept their homes, against about one-third of the control group, and received payments or rent waivers worth 9.4 months of rent against 1.9; the clients were chosen by the provider's selective intake.
anchor: Approximately two-thirds of occupants in the treated group, versus about one-third of occupants in the control group, retained possession of their units at the end of litigation.
treated-group occupants received payments or rent waivers worth on average a net of 9.4 months of rent per case, versus 1.9 months of rent per case in the control group.
a clientele recruited and chosen by the legal aid provider’s proactive, timely, specific, and selective outreach and intake system — an offer of full representation mattered.
locator: Introduction/summary, p. 1 of PDF text; Introduction/summary
context: Peer-reviewed randomized trial (Harvard Law Review, 2013).

statement: In a companion randomized trial in a Massachusetts Housing Court, an offer of full representation rather than limited help had no statistically significant effect on any substantive outcome, despite about 12.4 hours of attorney work per case against 1.7; rent savings were 1.8 against 1.6 months.
anchor: We find no statistically significant evidence that the Provider’s offer of full, as opposed to limited, representation had a large (or any) effect on any outcome of substantive import.

Tenants who received an offer of representation received approximately 12.4 hours of total attorney work per case, while tenants who received limited or unbundled assistance received only 1.7 hours per case
resulted in savings to the tenant of 1.8 months of rent on average, versus limited or unbundled assistance resulting in a savings to the tenant of 1.6 months of rent
context: Randomized trial, working paper (SSRN 1880078), by the authors of EV-HOU-143. It compares full representation with limited help, not with no help.

statement: Under New York City's Universal Access program, which offers free lawyers in housing court to tenants at or below 200 percent of the poverty guideline, tenants who gain lawyers are less likely to face possessory judgments, eviction warrants and eviction, and face smaller money judgments; effects are larger in poorer places.
anchor: The program offers free legal representation in housing court to tenants with income at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty guideline. We find that tenants who gain lawyers are less likely to be subject to possessory judgments, face smaller monetary judgments, are less likely to have eviction warrants issued against them, and are less likely to be evicted.
Lawyers have larger effects in poorer places and in those with larger shares of noncitizens.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Public Economics, 2023); uses the ZIP-code rollout.

statement: In the earliest New York City ZIP codes to get the right to counsel, legal representation rose and the share of filings ending in executed warrants fell, but only slightly.
anchor: We find relative increases in legal representation for treated ZIP Codes after the adoption of UAC. We also see small relative (and absolute) reductions in the share of filings resulting in executed warrants after UAC was implemented in the earliest ZIP Codes.
context: Peer-reviewed (Housing Policy Debate, 2021), NYU Furman Center.

statement: Nationally, tenants have lawyers in about 4% of eviction cases and landlords in 83%. In New York City, legal assistance lengthened cases by nearly three months and cut eviction orders by 32 percentage points, but listed rents rose by $29.1 to $38.1 a month in the second year of the right to counsel (1.2-1.6 percent), enough, the authors estimate, to cause a small net reduction in tenants' welfare.
anchor: an average representation rate of 4% for tenants and 83% for landlords
legal assistance increases case durations by nearly three months and reduces eviction orders by 32 percentage points.

In our main empirical specifications, we estimate an increase ranging from $6.5 (95% CI: [-6.5,19.4]) to $12.5 (95% CI: [1.3,23.8]) per month in the first year, and ranging from $29.1 (95% CI: [13.3,45.0]) to $38.1 (95% CI: [22.9,53.3]) per month in the second year.
amounting to a 1.2–1.6 percent price increase.
we estimate that the price increases due to RTC are large enough to more than offset the benefits to tenants, causing a small net reduction in their welfare.
locator: Introduction, p. 1; Introduction, p. 1-2; Introduction, p. 2
context: Working paper (2026) by Notre Dame, Yale, Chicago Booth and NYU economists; not yet peer-reviewed.

statement: In a calibrated model, a right to counsel drives up rents so much that homelessness rises by 15%, while rental assistance reduces homelessness by 45% and evictions by 75% and raises welfare despite its cost to taxpayers.
anchor: I find that “Right-to-Counsel” drives up rents so much that homelessness increases by 15% and welfare is dampened.
In contrast, rental assistance lowers tenants’ default risk and as a result reduces homelessness by 45% and evictions by 75%. It increases welfare despite its costs to taxpayers.
context: Structural model (job market paper, 2021); results rest on its assumptions, not on measured outcomes. Cited by critics of right to counsel.

statement: Cleveland's right to counsel raised the share of tenants represented in eviction cases from about 2% to 3% to about 16%; clients met 86% of goals to prevent eviction or an involuntary move, and the evaluators estimate $11.8 million to $14 million of local benefits from July 2020 through December 2022 on a $4.5 million investment.
anchor: the percentage of all tenants who are represented in landlord-tenant proceedings in Cleveland has increased from approximately 2% to 3%, before RTC-C, to approximately 16% since RTCC was implemented.
Prevent eviction or involuntary move 86%

Cleveland and Cuyahoga County likely realized combined economic benefits of between $11.8 million and $14 million from July 1, 2020 through December 31, 2022. During the same period, the total investment in RTC-C was $4.5 million19, resulting in an estimated return on investment of between $2.62 and $3.11.
locator: Key Evaluation Findings, p. 1; Client Goal Metrics table; Public Economic and Fiscal Benefits
context: Commissioned by the program's funder and provider; descriptive, without a comparison group; benefits rest on the evaluator's assumptions.

statement: Congress funded Emergency Rental Assistance with $25 billion and then $21.550 billion. By May 2021 only $1.5 billion (about 6%) of the first round had been spent, a rate generally considered too slow; after Treasury let applicants self-attest, spending in June 2021 doubled. Grantees reached 5.35 million households, most at or below 30% of area median income, and more than $3.1 billion of first-round funds was redirected from slow grantees.
anchor:
initially funded the ERA program with
an appropriation of $25 billion.

A second appropriation for ERA—of
$21.550 billion—was included in Section 3201 of the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021

$1.5
billion (about 6% of total ERA-1 funds) had been expended on rent and utility payments, an
expenditure rate that was generally considered to be too slow.

After the FAQ release, in June 2021, ERA-1
expenditures doubled compared to May 2021

grantees had provided ERA to 5.35
million unique households, the majority of which had incomes at or below 30% of local area median income.
redirecting more than $3.1 billion in ERA-1 funding
context: Nonpartisan legislative-branch agency.

statement: Emergency Rental Assistance, nearly $45 billion, sent more money per renting household to census tracts with higher pre-pandemic eviction filing rates, poverty rates and shares of Black renters, renters with children and single mothers; but its spending rose sharply around the end of the federal eviction moratorium, when filings were rising, which may confound causal estimates.
anchor: which provided nearly $45 billion to prevent evictions

we find that ERA sent more
funds per renting household to census tracts with higher pre-pandemic eviction filing rates,
higher poverty rates, higher shares of Black renters, higher shares of renting households with
children, and higher shares of renting single mothers.

ERA spending increased substantially around the expiration of the federal
eviction moratorium and at a time when eviction filings were increasing, which may confound
quasi-experimental analysis of ERA.
context: Federal Reserve Board working paper (FEDS 2024-055) by Treasury and Fed staff; Treasury ran the program.

statement: A HUD-funded evaluation finds eviction filings from March 2020 to early 2022 ran about 45% below pre-pandemic trends, roughly 673,000 fewer, the combined effect of moratoriums, state protections and rental assistance. Programs that verified eligibility with neighborhood data instead of tenant paperwork prevented more evictions; in Philadelphia, assistance cut the odds of homelessness by 60%, and in Los Angeles recipients were 65% less likely to end up on the street. Landlord-initiated applications were 30 percentage points more likely to succeed.
anchor: actual eviction filings between March 2020 and early 2022 ran approximately 45% below what pre-pandemic trends would have predicted — roughly 673,000 fewer filings . That gap reflects the combined force of federal moratoriums, state-level protections, and Emergency Rental Assistance.

Programs that verified eligibility using neighborhood-level data — instead of requiring tenants to produce pay stubs and hardship documentation — prevented more evictions, especially where funding was high.
In Philadelphia, ERA reduced the odds of moving by 35% and the odds of homelessness by 60%.
65% less likely to end up on the street
In Philadelphia, landlord-initiated applications were 30 percentage points more likely to succeed.
locator: How Much ERA Reduced Evictions; Key Findings; What the Household Studies Found; What the Household Studies Found (Los Angeles)
context: UC Berkeley and University of Pennsylvania researchers under HUD contract; published April 2026, under the second Trump administration, and under review; the summary is written in an advocacy tone. Observational county data and household surveys. As second-Trump-administration-era analysis without independent support for its delivery findings, it does not carry a recommendation on its own.

statement: Lotteries in five assistance programs that distributed over $200 million show that assistance increased rent payment and reduced concerns about eviction, but had little effect on housing stability or financial distress; the authors point to eviction moratoria, an expanded safety net and a softening market.
anchor: We evaluate five programs distributing over $200 million through lottery, using administrative and survey data to assess effects on rent payment, housing stability, financial distress, and health.
Assistance led to increases in rent payment and reduced concerns about eviction, with suggestive improvements in self-reported mental and physical health.

In contrast with pre-pandemic emergency rental assistance, we find little effect on housing stability or financial distress. Explanations for these muted effects include: eviction moratoria weakening the link between rent and displacement, expanded safety net programs, and market softening favoring tenants.
context: Randomized lotteries (NBER Working Paper 32463, issued May 2024, revised October 2025).

statement: Treasury's inspector general found that Treasury had wrongly concluded in its fiscal 2023 risk assessments that Emergency Rental Assistance was not susceptible to improper payments, when it likely was.
anchor:
RMA identified OCA, formerly ORP,
management inadequately concluded that the ERA and PSP programs are not susceptible to IPs in
their risk assessments completed for FY 2023 reporting, when these programs are likely
susceptible to IPs.
context: Audit by a contractor for Treasury's inspector general (2024, Biden administration; inspectors general report independently of agency leadership). So there is no official improper-payment rate for the program, and fraud claims can be neither confirmed nor sized from Treasury's reporting.

statement: When the UK cut Housing Benefit for new claimants, benefit receipt fell 10-15% and rents paid fell 6-11%, implying that between 60% and two-thirds of the cut fell on landlords.
anchor: We show that the changes did have an effect on the level of housing subsidy with an estimated fall of 10–15% in benefit receipt in the treatment group relative to the control group. There is also evidence that rents paid fell by 6–11%.
Our estimates imply that between 60% and two-thirds of the incidence of the subsidy reduction was on landlords.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Public Economics, 2006). UK Housing Benefit is an entitlement for a large share of renters, unlike rationed U.S. vouchers.

statement: When France extended housing benefits to all low-income households, one additional euro of benefit raised rents paid by new claimants by 78 cents, leaving 22 cents to lower their net rent; the author attributes this to a very low housing supply elasticity.
anchor: one additional euro of housing benefit leads to an increase of 78 cents in the rent paid by new benefit claimants, leaving only 22 cents available to reduce their net rent and increase their consumption.
This large impact of housing benefit on rents appears to be the result of a very low housing supply elasticity.
context: Peer-reviewed (Labour Economics, 2006).

statement: In France, housing subsidies raised rents overall between 2000 and 2016, even for unsubsidized tenants, since 40% of private tenants are subsidized; they also increased the quantity of private rentals. The subsidies cost EUR 15.7 billion in 2021, 0.6% of GDP.
anchor: Between 2000 and 2016, housing subsidies had an overall positive impact on rents, even for tenants that were not subsidised.
given that 40% of tenants in the private sector are subsidised, a landlord can take housing subsidies into account when setting the rent
This inflationary impact is accompanied by an increase in the quantity of private rental housing; no effect on quality is detected
in 2021 accounted for total expenditure of EUR 15.7 billion in France, or 0.6% of GDP
locator: section 'An overall upward long-term effect on rents'; same section; section 'Housing subsidies, a major tool of housing policy'
context: Banque de France researchers' summary (2023) of their working paper.

statement: In Finland, where the housing allowance jumps at unit-size and building-age cut-offs, rents show no matching jumps: differences in the allowance pass roughly one-to-one into lower net rent, and the upper bound of the effect on rent of 1 euro more allowance is about 0.2 euros.
anchor: However, our results show that there are no discontinuities in rents of the recipient households at these cut-offs. Instead, differences in the amount of the housing allowance are translated roughly one-to-one into differences in the rent net of housing allowance.
The upper limit of the 95% confidence interval for our preferred estimate for the effect of a 1 euro higher housing allowance is about 0.2 euros.
context: VATT and LSE discussion paper, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Economics. It measures within-market differences, not the effect on the overall rent level.

statement: Public spending on housing allowances is 1.4% of GDP in the United Kingdom, the highest in the OECD, close to 0.5% in Germany and the Netherlands, and between 0.1 and 0.3% of GDP in the United States, where the Housing Choice Voucher program is counted.
anchor: At 1.4% of GDP, public spending on housing allowances is by far the highest in the United Kingdom followed by Finland, Denmark and France

Public spending on housing allowances is close to 0.5% of GDP in Germany, the Netherlands and New Zealand, and between 0.1 and 0.3% of GDP in Australia, Czechia, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Norway, Sweden, and the United States.
context: OECD compilation of country data.

statement: In Austria, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands and Sweden, over 50% of bottom-fifth households report receiving a housing allowance; in the middle fifth the share is generally less than 10%.
anchor: In Austria, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands and Sweden, over 50% of households in the bottom quintile of the income distribution report receiving a housing allowance.
the share of households in the third income quintile receiving a housing allowance is generally less than 10%.
context: OECD compilation of survey data.

statement: Social housing is close to 28 million dwellings, 7% of the housing stock across the OECD; it exceeds 20% in Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands and is between 2 and 10% in the United States, Germany, Japan and Canada, among others.
anchor: Social housing represents close to 28 million dwellings and accounts on average for 7% of the total housing stock in the OECD (8% in the EU).
Accounting for over 20% of the total housing stock, the sector is largest in Austria, Denmark, and the Netherlands.

the sector is relatively small (between 2 and 10% of the total stock) in Australia, Belgium, Canada, Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Korea, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Switzerland, and the United States.
context: OECD compilation of country data.

statement: About 780,000 of Vienna's 1.86 million inhabitants lived in municipal and limited-profit housing in 2019. Tenants' down payments for new limited-profit housing became a barrier for low-skilled and vulnerable groups; main-residency rules exclude low-income newcomers and homeless people; and low turnover and growing demand mean long waiting lists.
anchor: In 2019 about 780,000 out of 1.86 million inhabitants lived in municipal and limited-profit housing
the tenants’ contributions for new subsidised social housing mainly built by LPHAs became a problematic barrier to low-skilled and vulnerable groups.
their recent reforms have also produced exclusions, especially for low-income newcomers in need or homeless persons that cannot fulfil the criteria of the main residency
although barriers to social housing based on citizenship have been removed, low turnover rates and growing demand for social housing explain long waiting lists
context: Peer-reviewed (Social Inclusion, 2021); University of Vienna sociologists.

statement: Social housing makes up 43% of all housing units in Vienna. Average rents are 7.9 EUR/m2 in limited-profit and 7.6 EUR/m2 in municipal housing, while average rents across the city rose from 7.5 EUR/m2 in 2012 to 10.7 EUR/m2 in 2022. A cited study finds a 10% higher limited-profit share lowers private rents by 30-40 cents/m2; land prices rose an average of 124% between 2010 and 2019.
anchor: The social housing sector comprises 43% of all housing units
Average social rental prices are significantly lower than in private rental, with 7.9 €/m2 in limited-profit housing and at 7.6 €/m2 in municipal housing
Average rental prices (regulated and unregulated) increased significantly in the last decade, from 7.5 €/m2 in 2012 to 10.7 €/m2 in 2022
an increase in the share of limited-profit housing by 10%, reduces rents by 30–40 cents/m2 in the private rental sector
Between 2010 and 2019, land prices increased by an average of 124%
locator: p. 4; p. 5; p. 8 (citing Klien et al., 2023)
context: Peer-reviewed (International Journal of Housing Policy, 2025); TU Wien and University of Vienna authors.

statement: The City of Vienna counts about 220,000 city-owned and 200,000 co-operative flats. To qualify, applicants must have lived at their current Vienna address for the past two years, and third-country nationals need more than five years of legal residence; longer-term residents get preference in allocation.
anchor: All in all, there are about 220,000 city-owned flats and 200,000 co-operative flats in Vienna
Vienna and your current flat must have been your primary place of residence throughout the past two years
a third country national (i.e. neither Austrian nor EU -citizen) who has had a valid residence permit for more than five years
People who have already been living in Vienna over a longer period of time will receive preferential treatment as far as allocation of flats is concerned.
locator: section 'Subsidised and city-owned flats'; Eligibility criteria
context: The city's own description of its stock and rules.

statement: Austrian employers and employees pay a housing tax of 1% of gross salaries, but none of it is now ring-fenced for housing. In 2021-2023 regional governments received about €1.2bn a year in returns on housing loans, enough to fund 60% of their roughly €2bn of annual housing spending, plus about €1.3bn from the tax, exceeding that spending by about €600m.
anchor: In all nine regions employers and employees pay a ‘housing tax’ totalling 1% of gross salaries (0.5% paid for by employers and 0.5% paid for by employees).

the average annual return to regional governments from outstanding loans amounted to €1.2bn in the years 2021-2023 (national aggregate). This means that 60% of the total public spend of around €2bn (average annual) in the period could be financed via returns on mortgages alone.
regional governments receive the proceeds from the housing tax, which currently amounts to about €1.3bn annually.
none of which is now ring-fenced for housing. This exceeds public spending by about €600m annually.
locator: p. 153; section 'A revolving public funding system?'; same section
context: Peer-reviewed (Critical Housing Analysis, 2025), but the authors work for the Austrian limited-profit housing federation and Housing Europe, the sector's associations.

statement: On 15 November 2024 Finland counted 3,806 homeless people living alone, 377 more than a year earlier and the first increase since 2012, and 1,010 long-term homeless; long-term homelessness decreased by about 70% between 2008 and 2024. The agency cautions that long-term figures should be taken with a grain of salt and that national totals are not fully comparable to those before 2018.
anchor: there were a total of 3,806 alone-living homeless people in Finland (situation on 15 November 2024). Of them, 1,010 were long-term homeless. There were 110 homeless families. Compared to the previous year, there were 377 more homeless people living alone
long-term homelessness decreased by about 70% between 2008 and 2024
This is the first time since 2012 when, based on the information submitted in the homelessness survey, the number of homeless people has increased from the previous year
The figures describing long-term homelessness should therefore be taken with a grain of salt. The actual number may be somewhat higher.
the figures for the number of homeless people in the whole country are not fully comparable to those prior to 2018.
context: Government agency that finances social housing; voluntary municipal reports. Finland counts people staying with friends or relatives, whom U.S. counts leave out.

statement: Finland's count of homeless single people fell from 17 110 in 1987 to 7 960 in 2008 through social housing and services, before its Housing First programme. Pleace notes Finland's unusual investment in social housing and that its welfare, health and housing systems already prevent much homelessness, leaving a smaller target.
anchor: In 1987, 17 110 single people and 1 370 families were recorded as homeless. Over the following decades, the social housing programme and the development of homelessness services had brought this number down considerably. In 2008, 7 960 single people and 300 families were recorded as homeless
Finland also has a level of investment in social housing, both in a financial and also political sense, that is not widespread in Europe.

Finland could be seen as having an ‘easier’ (or at least smaller) target in respect of tackling homelessness, because its welfare, health and housing systems, in and of themselves, already stop a lot of potential homelessness
context: Peer-reviewed (European Journal of Homelessness, 2017); a Housing First supporter.

statement: Long-term homelessness in Finland fell from approximately 3,500 to 1,000 between 2008 and 2020. Still, continued demand for emergency and temporary accommodation in large cities shows the model is less than fully effective, and its success is partly explained by long-term homelessness being a smaller problem in Finland than in many other OECD countries.
anchor: The estimated number of long-term homeless people has decreased from approximately 3,500 to 1,000 between 2008 and 2020

Perhaps the most serious indicator that the model is less than fully effective in eradicating long-term homelessness remains the continued demand for emergency housing services and temporary accommodation in the large Finnish cities.

the success of the Finnish implementation of the HF model is partly explained by long-term homelessness not being such a massive social problem in Finland in the first place, certainly when compared to many other OECD countries.
locator: p. 495; section on conflicted success; section on lessons
context: Peer-reviewed open-access chapter (Oxford University Press, 2022); Tampere University authors, in a volume on policy successes.

statement: The leaders of Finland's main Housing First provider report that lone homelessness fell 45% after 2008 and 75% since 1987; they name more affordable social housing, especially for people under 30, as the most important structural element of prevention, and call the residents Housing First does not reach 'the 10-20%'.
anchor: The total number of people experiencing homelessness and who live alone has decreased by 45% since the beginning of the first national programme in 2008, and by 75% since 1987
The most important structural element of prevention has been the increase in affordable social housing supply, especially social housing targeted at young people under the age of 30.
This group, which has been labelled the ‘10-20%’, is without a doubt the common development target in all countries implementing Housing First.
context: European Journal of Homelessness (2021); the authors lead the Y-Foundation, an interested party.

statement: 68% of the 4 600 lone homeless adults in Finland's count were staying temporarily with friends or relatives; Finland's statistics mix administrative data and estimates and do not provide a roadmap for comparison across countries.
anchor: 68% of the 4 600 lone homeless adults were living ‘temporarily with friends or relatives’

Finland’s national statistics are a mix of local authority administrative data and estimates, so that while they provide at least some sense of scale, the Finnish counts do not provide a roadmap for wider, comparative analysis
context: Peer-reviewed (European Journal of Homelessness, 2020).

statement: Germany's rent brake (Mietpreisbremse) dampened rent growth by up to 5% (up to 9% for some dwelling types), but the effect disappeared about a year after introduction, and it was strongest in higher-priced neighborhoods, missing its policy goal.
anchor: dass die Entwicklung der Mietpreise nach Einführung der Mietpreisbremse tatsächlich signifikant um bis zu 5 % (bis zu 9 % für bestimmte Wohnungstypen) gedämpft wurde. Der Effekt verschwindet jedoch etwa ein Jahr nach der Einführung und hat danach praktisch keine Auswirkungen mehr auf die Mietpreise.
Die stärksten Effekte hat die Mietpreisbremse insbesondere in höherpreisigen Nachbarschaften erzielt und verfehlt damit ihr ursprüngliches politisches Ziel.
context: Peer-reviewed (Regional Science and Urban Economics, 2022), RWI Essen; quoted from the German abstract.

statement: In HUD's 2024 count, 13 local homelessness systems reported increases due to immigrants or refugees seeking asylum. In New York City, asylum seekers in emergency shelters accounted for almost 88 percent of the increase in sheltered homelessness; in Chicago, new arrivals, including migrant and asylum-seeking families, accounted for more than 13,600 people in emergency shelters.
anchor:
Another 13 CoCs indicated an increase due to an increase in immigrants or refugees seeking
asylum.

asylum seekers in 2024. The CoC noted that these households, who were in emergency shelters,
accounted for almost 88 percent of the increase in sheltered homelessness in New York City.

new arrivals (which included migrant and asylum-seeking families,
including those bused or flown to Chicago from other states) accounted for more than 13,600 people in
emergency shelters in 2024.
context: HUD's 2024 homelessness report (Biden administration), reporting local Continuums of Care's own attributions of their increases: their analysis, not a measured share.

statement: In Germany, staggered adoption of the rent brake had a robust positive spillover effect on rents in the uncontrolled market, and households in rent-controlled units consumed more housing.
anchor: We find a robust positive spillover effect of rent control on free-market rents. Moreover, housing services consumption of households living in rent-controlled units increased.
context: Working paper (Erlangen-Nuremberg and DIW Berlin authors).

statement: Across U.S. communities, more investment in permanent supportive housing had modest negative associations with chronic homelessness: in the last study year, one more unit per 10,000 adults went with roughly 3 percent less chronic homelessness, and 0.4 percent using the previous year's units.
anchor: The results show modest negative associations between increased investment in PSH and rates of chronic homelessness over time.
in the last year of the study period, an increase of 1 PSH unit per 10,000 adults in a community is associated with roughly a 3 percent decrease in its total rate of chronic homelessness.
an increase in the lagged PSH measure of one PSH unit per 10,000 adults is associated with a 0.4 percent decrease in the total rate of chronic homelessness.
context: Peer-reviewed (Social Service Review, 2014); authors include a long-time supporter of permanent supportive housing.

statement: Each additional HUD-VASH voucher for veterans increased permanent supportive housing units by 0.9 and reduced the number of homeless veterans by 1; the authors conclude veteran homelessness would have risen substantially without the program.
anchor: For each additional voucher, permanent supportive housing units increased by 0.9 and the number of homeless veterans decreased by 1.
Our results indicate the HUD-VASH program worked as intended and veterans' homelessness would have risen substantially over the past decade without the program.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Journal of Public Health, 2019); Notre Dame authors. Evans also co-authored EV-HOU-108.

statement: Land-use reforms that loosened restrictions were associated with a 0.8 percent increase in housing supply within three to nine years, mostly at the higher end of the rent distribution, with no significant evidence that lower-cost units became more available or cheaper; tightening reforms were associated with higher median rents.
anchor: We find that reforms that loosen restrictions are associated with a statistically significant 0.8 percent increase in housing supply within three to nine years of reform passage, accounting for new and existing stock.

This increase occurs predominantly for units at the higher end of the rent price distribution; we find no statistically significant evidence that additional lower-cost units became available or became less expensive in the years following reforms.
reforms that increase land-use restrictions and lower allowed densities are associated with increased median rents
context: Urban Institute (center-left, nonpartisan) report, 2023, later in Urban Studies. Freemark (EV-HOU-124) is a co-author.

statement: From 1985-2011 panel data, homes filter down to lower-income occupants at a real annual rate of 2.5 percent for rentals and 0.5 percent for owner-occupied homes, more slowly where house prices rise faster; for most locations filtering is robust, which the author says supports housing vouchers.
anchor: I fill this gap by estimating a "repeat income" model using 1985-2011 panel data.

Real annual filtering rates are faster for rental housing (2.5 percent) than owner-occupied (0.5 percent), vary inversely with the income elasticity of demand and house price inflation, and are sensitive to tenure transitions as homes age.
For most locations, filtering is robust which lends support for housing voucher programs.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Review, 2014).

statement: Filtering rates range from about 1.61% a year downward in Topeka to 0.71% a year upward in San Francisco: markets with inelastic housing supply filter up on average, mostly because of faster house price growth.
anchor: these filtering rates can range from about a 1.61% annual rate of downward filtering for Topeka, Kansas to a 0.71% upward filtering rate for San Francisco, California.
MSAs with elastic housing supply have faster downward filtering than the national average whereas markets with inelastic housing supply have upwards filtering on average.
most of this difference can be explained by the higher house price growth on average in inelastic markets.
locator: working paper, introduction p. 1; working paper, introduction
context: Peer-reviewed (Regional Science and Urban Economics, 2022), Freddie Mac economists; quoted from the 2020 working paper.

statement: Ending rent control in Cambridge, Massachusetts, added about $1.8 billion to the value of the city's housing between 1994 and 2004, nearly a quarter of its residential price appreciation; spillovers to never-controlled properties nearby accounted for more than half of it.
anchor: we find that rent control's removal produced large, positive, and robust spillovers onto the price of never-controlled housing from nearby decontrolled units.

Elimination of rent control added about $1.8 billion to the value of Cambridge's housing stock between 1994 and 2004, equal to nearly a quarter of total Cambridge residential price appreciation in this period. Positive spillovers to never-controlled properties account for more half of the induced price appreciation.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Political Economy, 2014); quoted from NBER Working Paper 18125.

statement: St. Paul's 2021 rent control caused property values to fall 6-7%, an aggregate loss of $1.6 billion, a third of it from indirect effects; the tenants who gained most had higher incomes and were more likely to be white, while the owners who lost most had lower incomes and were more likely to be minorities.
anchor: We use the price effects caused by the passage of rent control in St. Paul, Minnesota in 2021

we find that rent control caused property values to fall by 6-7%, for an aggregate loss of $1.6 billion. A calibrated model of house prices under rent control attributes a third of these losses to indirect, negative externalities.
the tenants who gained the most from rent control had higher incomes and were more likely to be white, while the owners who lost the most had lower incomes and were more likely to be minorities.
context: NBER working paper (2022), USC economists.

anchor:
Section 301 amends the statutory definition of a “manufactured home” to provide that the home
may be “with or without a permanent chassis.” This section also directs HUD to issue revised
standards for such homes, including a requirement for a distinct label to distinguish manufactured
homes built with and without a permanent chassis. Additionally, this section provides that states
shall certify to HUD, not later than one year after enactment (July 11, 2027) (or two years after
enactment for states with legislatures that meet biennially), that they have amended their laws and
regulations to treat manufactured homes with and without a permanent chassis the same.
Section 301 also requires the HUD Secretary to adopt minimum energy efficiency standards for
manufactured homes not later than one year after enactment (July 11, 2027) and to update those

statement: CRS: HUD may run an escrow-only Family Self-Sufficiency pilot with up to 25 agencies or owners and up to 5,000 low-income families, ending July 11, 2036.
anchor:
Section 404 authorizes the HUD Secretary to create a new Escrow Expansion Pilot within the
FSS program that would allow families to participate in a streamlined version of FSS featuring
only the escrow account component of the program, without the caseworker and self-sufficiency
plan requirements. Under this section, HUD would select not more than 25 eligible entities
(PHAs or owners/sponsors of a multifamily property receiving project-based rental assistance) to
establish escrow accounts for not more than 5,000 low-income families. Section 404 requires the
HUD Secretary to select eligible entities not later than one year after establishing the pilot
program and to conduct a study and submit to Congress a report on outcomes not later than 10
years after selecting eligible entities. The termination date for the pilot program is 10 years after
enactment (July 11, 2036).

statement: Source of income is not a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act, which covers race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status and disability. Only a limited number of federal statutes and regulations bar landlords from refusing voucher holders, for example in certain HOME, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit and HUD-sold multifamily properties. Federal voucher rules do not preempt state or local protections.
anchor:
While source of income is not an expressly protected attribute under the Fair Housing Act 1, states or
localities are not precluded by Federal law from expanding discrimination protections to explicitly include
a person’s source of income, such as a housing choice voucher. No HUD housing choice voucher
regulations within 24 CFR 982 are intended to pre-empt the operation of state or local laws prohibiting
discrimination against voucher holders. Additionally, at the Federal level, a limited number of statutes
and regulations prohibit landlords from refusing to lease to voucher holders. For example, such
restrictions apply to certain properties supported under the HOME Investment Partnership Program,
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, and subsidized multifamily properties purchased from HUD.

The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion,
sex, familial status, and disability.
context: HUD Office of Inspector General audit, August 2025, second Trump administration. A count of enacted laws (data), graded A; the audit makes no recommendations.

statement: As of January 2025, 23 states and the District of Columbia had statewide laws making source of income a protected class, 16 of them explicitly protecting housing choice voucher holders; 152 cities and counties in 27 states had local ordinances, including in 19 states without a statewide law.

statement: Soltas: for every ten LIHTC units, about eight displace private housing that would have been built within ten years; LIHTC has added about 500,000 units, and its fiscal cost is about $1 million per net new unit.

Due to displacement, the fiscal cost of the LIHTC is about $1 million per net new unit on average.
context: Working paper (MIT job-market paper, 2024), not peer-reviewed; quasi-random award outcomes and scoring-rule nonlinearities. Agrees with the peer-reviewed crowd-out studies.

statement: In a meta-analysis of cohort studies, all-cause deaths per thousand person-years were 11.3 in methadone treatment against 36.1 out of it, and 4.3 against 9.5 for buprenorphine; the weeks starting methadone and right after leaving either treatment carry higher risk.
anchor: Pooled all cause mortality rates were 11.3 and 36.1 per 1000 person years in and out of methadone treatment (unadjusted out-to-in rate ratio 3.20, 95% confidence interval 2.65 to 3.86) and reduced to 4.3 and 9.5 in and out of buprenorphine treatment (2.20, 1.34 to 3.61).
The induction phase onto methadone treatment and the time immediately after leaving treatment with both drugs are periods of particularly increased mortality risk
context: Peer-reviewed (BMJ, 2017); observational cohorts, so confounding is possible, as the authors note. Spanish and EU public funders; no developer stake.

statement: The National Academies concluded that people with opioid use disorder are up to half as likely to die when treated long term with methadone or buprenorphine, and that the absence of counseling is not a reason to withhold the medications.
anchor: people with OUD are up to 50 percent less likely to die when they are being treated long term with methadone or buprenorphine.
A lack of availability of behavioral interventions is not a sufficient justification to withhold medications to treat opioid use disorder.
context: National Academies consensus report (2019), requested by NIDA and SAMHSA; synthesizes trials and cohort studies.

statement: A systematic review found that take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for a causal effect and reduces overdose deaths among participants and in the community, with few adverse events.
anchor: met all nine Bradford Hill criteria.
Take‐home naloxone programmes are found to reduce overdose mortality among programme participants and in the community and have a low rate of adverse events.
context: Peer-reviewed (Addiction, 2016) narrative synthesis of 22 observational studies. Conflict to weigh: the authors' university holds naloxone intellectual property and Strang has been paid by makers of naloxone products.

statement: CDC reports that people who use syringe services programs are five times as likely to enter drug treatment, and that decades of research find the programs safe, effective and cost saving without increasing drug use or crime.
anchor: SSP participants are 5 times more likely to enter drug treatment and 3.5 times more likely to cease injecting compared to those who don't utilize these programs.
Nearly 30 years of research has shown that comprehensive SSPs are safe, effective, and cost saving, do not increase illegal drug use or crime
context: CDC (Biden administration, 2024) summary of mostly observational research. The second Trump administration's July 2025 order bars SAMHSA discretionary grants for "harm reduction" efforts (EV-HOU-107, same order).

statement: A meta-analysis of 74 randomized trials with more than ten thousand adults on medication for opioid use disorder found contingency management (small rewards for negative drug tests) associated with abstinence from stimulants, other drugs and cigarettes, with a medium-to-large effect for stimulants.
anchor: In this systematic review and meta-analysis that included 74 randomized clinical trials and 10 444 adults receiving medication for opioid use disorder, the efficacy of contingency management was associated with abstinence from 4 types of substance use (psychomotor stimulants, polysubstance use, illicit opioids, and cigarettes)
stimulants, Cohen d = 0.70 [95% CI, 0.49-0.92]
context: Peer-reviewed (JAMA Psychiatry, 2021), NIH-funded; the senior author helped develop voucher-based contingency management. Effects are measured at the end of treatment, not long term.

statement: In the VA, 1,481 patients with stimulant use disorder who received contingency management were 41% less likely to die over a year than 1,481 matched patients who did not.
anchor: A total of 1,481 patients with StUD who received CM were included alongside 1,481 matched control subjects. Over the 1-year follow-up period, those who received CM were 41% less likely to die (adjusted hazard ratio=0.59, 95% CI=0.36, 0.95) than those who did not receive CM.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Journal of Psychiatry, 2025) matched cohort, not randomized; authors include the VA program lead. The interval is wide.

statement: In a Birmingham trial of 196 homeless cocaine users in day treatment, housing that required abstinence produced more abstinence than housing that did not, which in turn beat no housing; the authors recommend abstinence-contingent housing.
anchor: We studied 196 cocaine-dependent participants who received day treatment and no housing (NH), housing contingent on drug abstinence (ACH), or housing not contingent on abstinence (NACH).
The ACH group had a higher prevalence of drug abstinence than the NACH group (after control for treatment attendance), which in turn had a higher prevalence than the NH group.
context: Peer-reviewed randomized trial (AJPH, 2005) by the developers of the model. The housing was time-limited and the main outcome was abstinence, not long-term housing. This is the strongest evidence the treatment-first side cites.

statement: In a follow-up of the Birmingham trials, 34.1% of 138 participants had stable housing at 12 months; most did not, partly because local housing programs would not take people who had not achieved perfect abstinence.
anchor: Of 138 participants, the percentages with stable housing and employment at 12 months were 34.1 and 33.3%, respectively.

The majority of participants, however, did not achieve housing or employment, in part because of the limited capacity of the local housing programs to accommodate persons who had not achieved perfect abstinence.
context: Peer-reviewed (2007) by the same team as EV-HOU-306, so not independent of it.

statement: In randomized trials, assertive community treatment (a team that provides most care itself, around the clock) reduced homelessness 37% more and psychiatric symptoms 26% more than standard case management for homeless people with severe mental illness; hospital use did not differ.
anchor: In randomized trials, assertive community treatment subjects demonstrated a 37% (95% CI=18%-55%) greater reduction in homelessness and a 26% (95% CI=7%-44%) greater improvement in psychiatric symptom severity compared with standard case management treatments.
Hospitalization outcomes were not significantly different between the two groups.
context: Peer-reviewed meta-analysis (American Journal of Psychiatry, 2007); academic authors with no developer stake known.

statement: A systematic review found intensive case management reduced days homeless and substance use, assertive community treatment and critical time intervention protected against rehospitalization and looked promising for housing, and standard case management had limited, short-term effects.
anchor:
Intensive case management substantially reduced
the number of days spent homeless (SMD -0.22 95% CI -0.40 to -0.03), as well
as substance and alcohol use. Critical time interventions and assertive
community treatment were found to have a protective effect in terms of
rehospitalizations and a promising effect on housing stability.

Standard case management had both limited and short-term effects
on substance use and housing outcomes and showed potential to increase
hostility and depression.
context: Peer-reviewed (PLOS ONE, 2020) review of 56 studies for a Canadian clinical guideline; certainty varied by outcome. An earlier review (de Vet and others, 2013, not in the register) found standard case management helped substance users.
