context: HHS report to Congress (second Trump administration, 2025) on an independent Mathematica and RAND evaluation begun under earlier administrations; results vary by state and are not specific to homeless people. Presented as one source's view: no independent evaluation in the register.

statement: A review of recovery housing rated the evidence moderate: studies consistently showed positive outcomes, but they were few (six trials or quasi-experiments), small and single-site.
anchor: They identified six individual articles from 1995 through 2012 that reported on randomized controlled trials or quasi-experimental studies; no reviews or meta-analyses were found.
The level of evidence for recovery housing was moderate. Studies consistently showed positive outcomes, but the results were tempered by research design limitations
context: Peer-reviewed (Psychiatric Services, 2014), part of a SAMHSA-funded evidence series. Its main trial is an Oxford House study of people leaving treatment, not specifically homeless people. Presented as one source's view.

statement: SAMHSA recommends that recovery housing put no barriers on residents' use of prescribed medications, including for addiction.
anchor: SAMHSA recommends that recovery housing operators not have any barriers or restrictions for residents to use prescribed medications for behavioral or physical health conditions.
context: Federal guidance (SAMHSA, Biden administration, 2023); describes a recommended practice, not an outcome.

statement: A systematic review of nine studies of compulsory drug treatment found that, on the whole, it did not improve outcomes, and some studies suggested harm.
anchor: Of an initial 430 potential studies identified, nine quantitative studies met the inclusion criteria.
Evidence does not, on the whole, suggest improved outcomes related to compulsory treatment approaches, with some studies suggesting potential harms.
context: Peer-reviewed (International Journal of Drug Policy, 2016) by harm-reduction researchers; partly funded by the Open Society Foundations. Includes drug detention centers abroad, unlike U.S. court-mandated community treatment.

statement: In a VA cohort of 2,095 patients, those mandated to treatment by courts had similar or better 1- and 5-year outcomes than voluntary patients, which the authors read as support for judicial mandates as a route into treatment.
anchor: This prospective study (n=2,095) examined differences in pretreatment characteristics, treatment perceptions and satisfaction, during-treatment changes, and 1- and 5-year outcomes
Mandated patients had a less severe clinical profile at treatment intake, yet this did not account for their observed similar/better outcomes
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment, 2005); VA researchers; not randomized and not specific to homeless people.

statement: The National Academies found no substantial published evidence, apart from people with HIV/AIDS, that permanent supportive housing improves health or cuts health costs, and advised policymakers not to expect net savings except perhaps among the heaviest users of emergency services.
anchor: except for some evidence that PSH improves health outcomes among individuals with HIV/AIDS, the committee finds that there is no substantial published evidence as yet to demonstrate that PSH improves health outcomes or reduces health care costs.
The committee does not believe policy makers and others should expect that permanent supportive housing programs would yield net cost savings
context: National Academies consensus report (2018); it notes supportive housing was designed to end chronic homelessness, not to save money. Predates the Denver and Santa Clara trials.

statement: In a Santa Clara County trial of 423 chronically homeless frequent users of public services, Eighty-six percent of those offered supportive housing were housed against 36 percent with usual care; psychiatric emergency visits and shelter days fell, but total emergency, inpatient and jail use did not change.
anchor: We enrolled 423 participants (199 intervention; 224 control). Eighty‐six percent of those randomized to PSH received housing compared with 36 percent in usual care. On average, the 169 individuals housed by the PSH intervention have remained housed for 28.8 months (92.9 percent of the study follow

Intervention group members had lower rates of psychiatric ED visits IRR 0.62; 95% CI [0.43, 0.91] and shelter days IRR 0.30; 95% CI [0.17, 0.53], and higher rates of ambulatory mental health services use IRR 1.84; 95% CI [1.43, 2.37] compared to controls. We found no differences in total ED or inpatient use, or jail.
context: Peer-reviewed randomized trial (Health Services Research, 2020) of a county pay-for-success project; more than a third of the control group got other subsidized housing, biasing results toward no effect.

statement: In the Denver supportive housing trial for frequent jail users, 79 percent of those referred were located, engaged and housed; 77 percent of living participants were still housed at three years, and total jail days fell 27 percent.
anchor: Of those in the treatment group, 79 percent (285 people) were located, engaged, and housed.
At year 3, the rate was 77 percent.
This represents a 30 percent reduction in unique jail stays and a 27 percent reduction in total jail days.
context: Urban Institute (2021), the initiative's independent evaluator; investors' payments depended on the outcomes. Randomized, intent-to-treat, administrative data; emergency medical use did not differ significantly.

statement: In Denver, about half of the yearly cost of supportive housing per person was offset by lower spending on other public services, $6,876 per person a year.
anchor: Approximately half the total annual per person cost of the Denver SIB was offset by reductions in the costs of other public services. The treatment group had $6,876 less in total annual per person costs associated with avoided outcomes compared with the control group.
context: Urban Institute (2021) cost study on the randomized trial; funded by Arnold Ventures; same team as EV-HOU-317.

statement: A review of Housing First cost studies found pre-post studies reported net savings but experimental studies reported net cost increases, so the programs may not pay for themselves, though their offsets and benefits make them an efficient use of resources.
anchor: Studies using a pre–post design reported a net decrease in overall costs with HF. In contrast, experimental studies reported a net increase in overall costs with HF.

While our review casts doubt on whether HF programs can be expected to pay for themselves, the certainty of significant cost offsets, combined with their benefits for participants, means that they represent a more efficient allocation of resources than traditional services.
context: Peer-reviewed review (Canadian Journal of Psychiatry, 2015); Latimer led the At Home/Chez Soi cost analysis.

statement: In Canada's At Home/Chez Soi trial, every $10 spent on Housing First saved an average of $9.60 for high-needs participants served by assertive community treatment and $3.42 for moderate-needs participants served by intensive case management.
anchor: every $10 invested in HF services resulted in an average savings of $9.60 for high needs/ ACT participants and $3.42 for moderate needs/ICM participants.
context: Final report of the randomized trial (Mental Health Commission of Canada, 2014), written by its investigators; Canadian costs.

statement: At Home/Chez Soi let participants choose their housing and supports but required them to meet a member of their support team at least once a week.
anchor: Participants had a choice around the housing and supports they needed, with a requirement that participants meet with a member of their support team at least once a week.
context: Program description in the trial's final report (Mental Health Commission of Canada, 2014).

statement: The original Pathways to Housing program had two requirements: tenants paid 30% of income toward rent through money management and met a staff member at least twice a month, applied flexibly.
anchor: There are 2 program requirements: tenants must pay 30% of their income (usually Supplemental Security Income [SSI]) toward the rent by participating in a money management program, and tenants must meet with a staff member a minimum of twice a month. These requirements are applied flexibly to suit consumers' needs.
context: Program description in the founding Housing First trial (AJPH, 2004); Tsemberis founded Pathways to Housing.

statement: The Pathways Housing First fidelity scale gives its top score to programs where tenants keep housing with no requirement beyond a standard lease and a weekly face-to-face visit with staff, and can refuse any other service.
anchor: Participants can keep their housing with no requirements for continued tenancy, other than adhering to a standard lease and seeing staff for a face-to-face visit once a week.
Participants have the right to choose, modify, or refuse services and supports at any time, except one face-to-face visit with staff a week.
context: Validated fidelity instrument (2013) by the model's founder and colleagues.

statement: SAMHSA's supportive housing fidelity scale gives full marks when tenancy is in no way contingent on program or treatment participation, a middle score when rules require ongoing services but noncompliance does not lead to eviction, and the lowest when tenancy is revoked for noncompliance.
anchor: Tenancy is not contingent in any way on compliance with program or treatment participation
Program rules require participating in ongoing services, but failure to comply with this requirement does not lead to eviction.
Tenancy is revoked based on noncompliance with program or failure to participate in treatment
locator: Evaluating Your Program, Appendix B, item 5.1.b
context: Federal practice standard (SAMHSA, Obama administration, 2010).

statement: HUD-VASH vouchers are conditioned on VA case management, not treatment; if the VA finds a veteran is not participating without good cause, the housing agency must end HUD-VASH assistance but may move the family to a regular voucher.
anchor:
As a condition of HCV rental assistance, both tenant-based voucher
and PBV, a HUD-VASH eligible veteran must receive the case management
services noted above, as needed, directly from or arranged by the VA.
The VA, in consultation with the veteran, is responsible for
determining if case management is required and if the case management
requirement is satisfied.

If the VA has determined that a veteran is not
participating in required case management, without good cause, the PHA
must terminate the family from the HUD-VASH program. However, the PHA
may offer the family continued assistance through one of its regular
vouchers or a PBV unit not exclusively made available for HUD-VASH.
context: Federal program notice (HUD, Biden administration, 2024); binding operating requirements.

statement: Under HUD-VASH, a VA finding that a veteran no longer needs case management is never grounds to end the voucher, and the VA stays in contact to help with recertification.
anchor:
A VA determination that the veteran does not require or no longer
requires case management is never grounds for termination of HCV
assistance.

If a veteran no longer requires case management, but maintains
their HUD-VASH voucher assistance, the VA will maintain contact with
the veteran family to provide support and planning assistance with the
recertification and reinspection process.
context: Federal program notice (HUD, Biden administration, 2024).

statement: Finland's Y-Foundation writes no sobriety or similar terms into leases; a tenant behind on rent who stops answering housing counsellors is reported to social services before any eviction begins.
anchor: Any terms are not included in the agreements, for instance sobriety.

A resident can be evicted due to overdue rent when they stop answering the housing counselling services' contacts after multiple attempts to contact them. If they cannot be reached, a notice of concern regarding the tenant is submitted to social welfare services. It is only after this that eviction steps into the picture.
context: Practitioner guide (Y-Foundation, 2022), Finland's largest nonprofit landlord for formerly homeless people; describes practice, not measured outcomes.

statement: In Washington's Medicaid-funded supportive housing services, exits from homelessness were about 4 percentage points higher than in a matched comparison group in the first evaluation; reductions in emergency and inpatient use were promising but not quite statistically significant.
anchor: The percentage of individuals transitioning out of homelessness as of the last month of the follow-up period was roughly 4 percentage points higher for both populations.
These impact estimates approached but did not quite achieve the usual standard of statistical significance.
context: State evaluation (Washington DSHS, 2020) funded by the agency that runs the program; matched comparison, short follow-up. Presented as one source's view.

statement: CMS approved Minnesota's request to terminate its Medicaid Housing Stabilization Services benefit effective November 1, 2025.
anchor:
The effective date for this amendment is November 1, 2025. With this amendment, the
state is terminating this benefit.
context: Federal approval letter (CMS, second Trump administration, 2025). Minnesota sought the termination after suspending payments to providers over credible allegations of fraud (state news release, not saved).

statement: Residents of Housing First programs were less likely than residents of other supportive housing to report that treatment was required to get or keep housing, with no difference in housing satisfaction.
anchor: those in housing-first programs were significantly less likely to report that mental health treatment adherence was an explicit requirement of obtaining housing and less likely to report that mental health and substance abuse treatment was a requirement of retaining housing. There was no difference between the programs in residents' satisfaction with their housing.
context: Peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey (Psychiatric Services, 2009) of 136 residents; it does not measure whether perceived coercion changes engagement.

statement: At Home/Chez Soi's Toronto site found the weekly-visit requirement may have hindered recovery for some participants, such as those with jobs or school who did not want to be seen with caseworkers.
anchor: The Toronto site found that the requirements of the program model for caseworkers to meet with participants weekly may have been an impediment to recovery processes for some.
did not want to be seen with caseworkers in their community.
context: Qualitative implementation evaluation by the trial team (Mental Health Commission of Canada).

statement: Continuum of Care rules let projects require participation in services that are not disability-related, such as case management, as a condition of staying in the program; they may require treatment only in projects whose purpose is substance abuse treatment.
anchor:
Recipients and subrecipients may require
the program participants to take part
in supportive services that are not disability-related
services
provided
through the project as a condition of
continued participation in the program.

Notwithstanding this provision, if the purpose
of the project is to provide substance
abuse treatment services, recipients
and subrecipients may require program
participants to take part in such services as a condition of continued participation in the program.
context: Federal regulation (HUD Continuum of Care interim rule, 2012; 2025 edition).

statement: The second Trump administration's HUD argues that Housing First never ruled out participation requirements, citing Pathways' original visits and HUD-VASH, and that chronic homelessness rose 80.5 percent since 2013 despite a 44 percent increase in supportive housing beds.
anchor:
the Evidence Matters report acknowledged that the first
program to implement Housing First--Pathways to Housing--initially
required program participants to agree to two staff visits per month.
This example illustrates that Housing First did not preclude
participation requirements.

HUD finds that HUD-VASH demonstrates the efficacy of housing
assistance tied to participation in case management and services.

chronic homelessness has increased 80.5 percent
since 2013 to the highest number on record despite a 44 percent
increase nationwide in Permanent Supportive Housing beds during the
same period.
context: HUD (second Trump administration, 2026), written to justify its FY2026 Continuum of Care scoring during litigation; the administration's view. Its trend figures are descriptive, not causal. Its point that the Pathways model expected staff contact matches the model's own rules (EV-HOU-322, EV-HOU-323); its conclusion against Housing First is contested by the trial evidence.

statement: HUD's FY2026 Continuum of Care competition sets aside $1.3 billion of $4.04 billion for transitional housing and services-only projects, and awards up to 20 of 200 points for treatment and recovery services and up to 8 for requiring participation in services; Congress required HUD to fund at least 60 percent of each community's renewals.
anchor: FY2026, $1.3 billion (of $4.04 billion in total funding) is set aside for

Of the 200 points available in the competition, up to 20 are for providing treatment and recovery services
and up to 8 for requiring participation in supportive services.
provided that HUD “shall select projects totaling not less than 60 percent of the [ARD]” for each
context: Congressional Research Service summary (nonpartisan, 2026) of the notice and appropriations law.

statement: The First Circuit stayed the district court's order vacating HUD's FY2026 Continuum of Care notice, finding HUD likely to win on the notice-and-comment question; HUD must make awards by December 1, 2026.
anchor:
HUD has made a strong
showing that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the district court's holding that
the set-aside in the NOFO was subject to notice and comment requirements pursuant to 42 U.S.C.
HUD only has until December 1, 2026
context: Federal appellate order (2026). The merits appeal and remaining district court claims were open as of this note.

statement: States must start Medicaid work requirements by January 1, 2027; CMS says homelessness alone does not make someone medically frail, though a substance use disorder or disabling mental disorder can.
anchor:
States are required to
implement the new requirement no later than January 1, 2027.

we do not believe
it would be reasonable for States to consider an individual who is
homeless as medically frail solely on the basis that the individual is
homeless, as that circumstance is not a medical condition. However,
individuals who are homeless may have a medical condition, such as an
SUD or disabling mental disorder, that could qualify them for the
medically frail exclusion.
context: Federal rule (CMS, second Trump administration, 2026), implementing Public Law 119-21.

statement: From January 1, 2027, CMS may approve or renew a Medicaid demonstration (waiver) only if its chief actuary certifies it will not raise federal spending.
anchor:
general.--Beginning January 1 2027, the Secretary may not
approve an application for (or renewal or amendment of) an
experimental, pilot, or demonstration project undertaken under
subsection (a) to promote the objectives of title XIX in a State
(in this subsection referred to as a `Medicaid demonstration
project') unless the Chief Actuary for the Centers for Medicare
& Medicaid Services certifies that such project, or, in the case
of a renewal, the duration of the preceding waiver, is not
expected to result in an increase in the amount of Federal
expenditures compared to the amount that such expenditures would
otherwise be in the absence of such project.
context: Enacted federal law (Public Law 119-21, sec. 71118).

statement: HRSA projects shortages at its projection horizon, under current trends, of 77,050 addiction counselors, 36,780 adult psychiatrists and 99,780 mental health counselors.
anchor: Addiction counselors | -77,050 (30%)
Adult psychiatrists | -36,780 (50%)
Mental health counselors | -99,780 (55%)
context: Federal workforce model (HRSA, second Trump administration, December 2025); model-based projections. Presented as one source's view; the 2024 edition projected larger shortages for 2037.

statement: In March 2025 CMS rescinded its 2023 and 2024 guidance on covering housing and other health-related social needs in Medicaid waivers, saying it would weigh state requests case by case.
anchor: CMS is rescinding the November 2023 and December 2024 CIBs.

case-by-case basis to
determine whether they satisfy federal requirements for approval under the applicable
provisions of the Social Security Act and implementing federal regulations, without reference
to the November 2023 and December 2024 CIBs or the HRSN Framework.
context: Federal guidance (CMS, second Trump administration, 2025). The bulletin is silent on waivers already approved.

statement: HUD's workforce fell by about 29 percent between December 2024 and December 2025, from about 8,800 to about 6,300 employees; over half of those who left had at least 10 years at HUD, including 41 percent with more than 20, and HUD hired 193 employees in 2025.
anchor: HUD’s workforce decreased by about 29 percent between December 2024 and December 2025, from about 8,800 to about 6,300 employees
Over half of the separated employees had worked at HUD for at least 10 years, including 41 percent who had over 20 years of service
from January 2025 to December 2025, HUD hired 193 employees
locator: Section 'HUD Lost 29 Percent of Its Staff', p. 8 and fig. 2
context: GAO (legislative branch), October 2026, counting OPM workforce data on the second Trump administration's 2025 reductions. HUD did not answer GAO's questions. Data, graded A.

statement: In fiscal year 2024, more than one-quarter of VA medical centers with two or more HUD-VASH case managers had at least 20 percent of those positions unfilled, and annual case manager turnover ran from 20 to 26 percent in fiscal years 2020-2024; staffing shortfalls reduced services and delayed admissions.
anchor: In fiscal year 2024, more than one-quarter of medical centers with two or more case managers had at least 20 percent of these positions unfilled
annual case manager turnover ranged from 20 percent to 26 percent in fiscal years 2020–2024
The effects of insufficient staffing include reduced services for veterans and delays in admitting new participants.
context: GAO (legislative branch), March 2026, analyzing VA staffing data for fiscal years 2020-2024 (first Trump and Biden administrations). Data, graded A.

statement: Of 174,045 instances of eligible veterans not being referred to HUD-VASH in 2020-2024, VA did not record the reason in 151,296 (87 percent), so it cannot measure how much case-manager shortages keep veterans out.
anchor: Of 174,045 instances of veterans not being referred to the program in 2020–2024, VA did not document the reason in 151,296 (87 percent), according to GAO’s analysis.
context: GAO, March 2026. Data, graded A.

statement: HUD estimated calendar-2026 administrative fees for Housing Choice Vouchers at 85% proration of what housing agencies are eligible for; Emergency Housing Voucher fees were funded at the full rate and not prorated.
anchor: Administrative fees for CY 2026 were estimated at 85% proration.

The Emergency Housing Voucher (EHV) program ongoing fees are funded at the HCV
program Column A rate and will not be prorated in CY 2026.
context: HUD notice, second Trump administration, 2026; the proration follows from the FY2026 appropriation Congress passed. NAHRO reported an 86% estimate in August 2026. Data, graded A.

statement: A year after Emergency Housing Vouchers were awarded, 87% were leased or issued; more than 26,000 households had leased and nearly 35,000 were searching, and the average time from issuance to lease was 77 days.
anchor: In the last year, EHVs have helped more than 26,000 households secure permanent housing, and nearly 35,000 are searching for a unit or completing the leasing process. 87% of EHVs have been either leased or issued , and on average, the time between an EHV being issued to leasing a home is 77 days.
context: USICH announcement, Biden administration, July 2022, with a stake in presenting the program well; the counts come from HUD's EHV dashboard. 'Leased or issued' counts vouchers still searching; the leased share alone was about a third of 70,000 (26,000). Data.

statement: As of February 2023, 67 percent of awarded Emergency Housing Vouchers were leased; 129 of 610 housing agencies had leased less than half of their vouchers, and only 62 had leased all of them.
anchor: As of February 21, 2023, 67 percent of awarded EHVs were leased
More than one fifth of PHAs that were awarded EHVs—129 of 610 PHAs—had leased less than half of their total EHV authority.
Only 62 PHAs have successfully managed to lease all of their EHVs.
context: Terner Center (UC Berkeley), March 2023, reading HUD's EHV dashboard; independent of the administration that ran the program. Data from HUD's counts, graded C as a secondary tabulation.

statement: Emergency Housing Vouchers, 70,000 vouchers allocated to 613 housing agencies in May 2021, helped more than 60,000 households into housing; as of April 2025, 59,323 were still leased. Interviewed agencies credited partnerships with Continuums of Care, existing case managers, separate waiting lists, at least 120 days to search, self-certification of documents and income, pre-inspection and higher payment standards.
anchor: In May 2021, HUD allocated 70,000 tenant-based vouchers to 613 public housing authorities (PHAs) across the country. The EHV program has helped move more than 60,000 households into housing, and as of April 2025, 59,323 vouchers are still leased.

the separate waiting lists for the EHV program, the extension of the minimum initial search term to at least 120 days, self-certification of identity documents and income during applications, preinspection of units, and a higher payment standard for EHVs.
context: Urban Institute (center-left research organization), April 2025: HUD counts plus 23 interviews in six communities. The counts are data; which features helped is the interviewees' account (analysis).

statement: Although the number of vouchers rose slightly from 2010 to 2016, the number of landlords in the Housing Choice Voucher program fell from just over 700,000 to around 640,000, raising vouchers per landlord from 2.6 to 3.1.
anchor: although the total number of vouchers increased slightly between 2010 and 2016, the number of landlords decreased from just over 700,000 to around 640,000, resulting in an overall increase in the number of vouchers per landlord from 2.6 vouchers per landlord in 2010 to 3.1 vouchers per landlord in 2016.
context: HUD PD&R study, first Trump administration, 2019, counting HUD's administrative (PIC) records. Data, graded A. The same study's interviews found housing agency staff named payment levels and paperwork, more than attitudes to tenants, as why landlords leave.

statement: In the Rental Assistance Demonstration evaluation's tenant survey, 82 percent of respondents stayed at the same property through conversion; after conversion 75 percent were back in their original unit, 92 percent in the original property, and just over 2 percent were no longer in subsidized housing.
anchor: we found that 82 percent of all respondents remained in the same throughout the RAD conversion process
75 percent were back in their original unit, 92 percent were in the original property, and almost 98 percent were receiving rental assistance of some kind
Just over 2 percent of respondents reported they were no longer in subsidized housing.
context: HUD-commissioned evaluation (Econometrica), first Trump administration, 2019. A survey of 298 residents of 18 early conversions, with a 31% enrollment rate; NLIHC (2019) counted 13 of the 18 in the South and notes the sample may not represent later conversions. HUD's data could not track movers. Survey data, graded C for the small, unrepresentative sample.

statement: In a 2023 survey of homeless services workers, 55 percent of full-time respondents earned under $50,000 a year, three in four said their organizations were understaffed, and 71 percent said high turnover was an issue at their jobs.
anchor: Of those responding (and working at leady 35 hours per week), 55 percent were making under $50,000 per year.
Three out of every four workers indicated that their organizations/agencies were understaffed
71 percent of respondents said that this was an issue at their jobs.
context: National Alliance to End Homelessness (advocacy organization), December 2023: a convenience survey of its own networks, not a random sample, and mostly college-educated respondents. Its summary also says 55 percent earned under $55,000; the salary table gives under $50,000, used here. Data with a stake in the answer, graded C.

statement: The first round of Emergency Rental Assistance set aside $0.800 billion for governments in tribal areas, allocated in proportion to FY2020 Native American Housing Block Grant payments; the second round had no tribal set-aside.
anchor: ERA-2 did not include a tribal set-aside
context: CRS (nonpartisan legislative-branch agency), January 2023, summarizing the enacted laws. Data.

statement: A housing agency may use for project-based vouchers not more than 20 percent of its authorized units, plus up to an additional 10 percent for homeless families, veterans, supportive housing and areas where vouchers are difficult to use.
anchor: a public housing agency may use for project-based assistance under this paragraph not more than 20 percent of the authorized units for the agency.
A public housing agency may use up to an additional 10 percent of the authorized units for the agency for project-based assistance under this paragraph
context: Primary law, as amended through 2026.

statement: A family in a project-based voucher unit may move at any time after 12 months and must be given tenant-based help, but if none is immediately available the agency may meet the duty by giving the family priority for the next voucher that becomes available.
anchor: may move from the housing at any time after the family has occupied the dwelling unit for 12 months.
such requirement may be met by providing the family priority to receive the next voucher or other tenant-based rental assistance amounts that become available
context: Primary law, as amended through 2026.

statement: At the end of 2023, 2404197 Housing Choice Voucher households were reported in 2752351 voucher units, 84% occupied; average HUD spending per voucher unit was $1068 a month.
anchor: Housing Choice Vouchers | total_units = 2752351
Housing Choice Vouchers | pct_occupied = 84
Housing Choice Vouchers | number_reported = 2404197
Housing Choice Vouchers | spending_per_month = 1068
note: HUD administrative data (Picture of Subsidized Households, U.S. total, Housing Choice Vouchers row). spending_per_month is HUD's average federal spending per unit per month; the extract does not say whether it includes the administrative fee, so section 6 treats it as the rent subsidy and adds fees separately (the cautious reading). Section 6 uses it as the 2023 base for the cost of a voucher-year.

By household type the worst case needs counts were 345 thousand families with children, 57 thousand older adult households, 175 thousand other family households and 585 thousand other nonfamily households (of 940, 154, 448 and 1,601 thousand).

statement: For 2023, the SSI monthly federal benefit rate for an individual living alone was $914.
anchor: For 2023, the SSI monthly federal benefit rate for an individual living alone is $914.
note: Footnote in HUD's Worst Case Housing Needs 2025 report, citing SSA. Section 6 uses it to judge that most very low-income disabled renter households living on SSI fall below the extremely low-income line.

statement: CBO estimated that a one-time 10 percent increase in vouchers would assist roughly 200,000 more households at $18 billion over ten years, and that offering vouchers over ten years to all households at or below 30 percent of area median income would assist roughly 4.5 million more at $290 billion.
anchor: CBO estimates that a onetime 10 percent increase in the number of vouchers would assist roughly 200,000 additional households and cause federal spending to increase by a total of $18 billion from 2016 through 2025.

offering vouchers gradually over a period of 10 years to all households with income of no more than 30 percent of AMI would ultimately assist roughly 4.5 million additional households at a cost of $290 billion from 2016 through 2025.
context: CBO budget option (2015), nonpartisan; a cost estimate, so analysis. Older price level than the plan.

statement: CBO estimated the federal government would spend $9,400 per year, on average, for each household receiving a voucher in 2019.
anchor: The federal government will spend $9,400 per year, on average, for each household that receives a voucher in 2019, CBO estimates.
context: CBO budget option (December 2018), nonpartisan projection.

statement: The Urban Institute estimates that full funding and use of vouchers would add 13.2 million assisted households and raise total housing subsidies from about $50 billion to $168 billion a year, an increase of $118 billion; newly assigned vouchers would average a $765 monthly subsidy.
anchor: this would increase by 13.2 million to a total of 17.6 million with full funding and use of housing vouchers
providing subsidies to all who are eligible would increase the total amount of subsidies paid by $118 billion, to a total of $168 billion
Currently assisted households receive about $50 billion in housing subsidies.
households assigned vouchers in our hypothetical scenario would receive an average subsidy of $765 per month.
context: Urban Institute (2023), TRIM/ATTIS microsimulation; a thought experiment assuming every eligible household applies and leases. Center-left research organization.

statement: Full funding and use of vouchers would cut the child poverty rate by 23 percent, with the largest poverty reduction for Hispanic people (19 percent), then Black non-Hispanic people (15 percent) and white non-Hispanic people (9 percent), in the Urban Institute simulation.
anchor: The child poverty rate would fall by 23 percent
Hispanic people would have the largest reduction in poverty (19 percent), followed by Black, non-Hispanic people (15 percent)
and white, non-Hispanic people (9 percent).
context: Urban Institute (2023) simulation; assumes full take-up and lease-up, no labor-supply response.

statement: The Urban Institute notes that the current 61 percent success rate in using vouchers would likely fall as more households sought to use them.
anchor: The current 61 percent success rate in using vouchers would likely fall as greater numbers of households sought to use vouchers.
context: Urban Institute (2023), stated as a caveat, not estimated.

statement: An American Community Survey measure counts 3,717,589 people (1.2% of the population) doubled up in 2019; 737,886 were school-age children, against the Education Department's 1.04 million doubled-up students over the 2018–2019 school year. statement: The 2008 HERA credit was refundable, worth 10% of price up to $7,500, phased out between $75,000 and $95,000 of income ($150,000-$170,000 joint), and had to be repaid over 15 years, making it an interest-free loan; ARRA raised it to $8,000 and dropped repayment; the WHBAA extension added a $6,500 credit for repeat buyers (five of the last eight years in the home), raised the income limits to $125,000/$225,000 and barred homes priced over $800,000.
anchor: Eligible buyers were allowed a refundable credit against their federal income tax equal to a maximum of 10% of a home's purchase price, or $7,500. The amount of the credit that could be claimed was reduced for individuals with modified adjusted gross income (AGI) of more than $75,000 ($150,000 for joint filers), and was zero for those individuals with modified AGI in excess of $95,000 ($170,000 for joint filers).
Those who claimed the 2008 first-time homebuyer tax credit must repay the tax credit in equal installments over 15 years beginning in the second taxable year after the purchase of a home.
the repayable tax credit equates to an interest free loan
The credit amount was set equal to a maximum of 10% of a home's purchase price, or $8,000. The tax credit remained refundable, although the repayment requirement was removed.

The tax credit for repeat buyers was capped at $6,500 and was limited to those who have owned and lived in their current home for five of the last eight years. Other changes included an expansion of the maximum credit income eligibility limits to $125,000 for individuals and $225,000 for married couples, up from $75,000 and $150,000, respectively. Lastly, an $800,000 limit on the purchase price of a home was included.
locator: Summary; "Overview of the Homebuyer Tax Credit"

statement: JCT estimated the HERA credit at $4.9 billion over 10 years, the ARRA changes at $6.5 billion and the WHBAA version at $10.8 billion; by CRS's count of early IRS data, 1.4 million first-time buyers had claimed about $10 billion (average $7,004), and CRS judged that most claimants were buyers who had already decided to purchase.

Thus far, 1.4 million first-time homebuyers have claimed approximately $10 billion worth of tax credits.
The average tax credit claimed was $7,004.
while the majority of the other claimants likely were buyers who had already decided to purchase a home, and simply claimed the tax credit because it was available.

context: Congressional Research Service, July 2010; nonpartisan; reports JCT estimates and preliminary IRS counts (through August 2009 purchases); the "majority anyway" judgment is CRS reasoning, not an estimate.

statement: Using price elasticities of -0.5 to -1.5, CRS estimated the ARRA credit could have been expected to add 42,790 to 128,371 home purchases and the WHBAA version 51,523 to 153,760, well below industry estimates.
anchor: Because estimates of the price elasticity vary, three different values were used; -0.5, -1.0, and -1.5.

Depending on the assumed responsiveness of buyers to price changes, it was estimated that the ARRA tax credit could have been expected to result in between 42,790 and 128,371 additional home purchases, while it was estimated that the WHBAA tax credit could be expected to result in between 51,523 and 153,760 additional purchases.
It is immediately apparent that private industry analysts' estimates are higher than those reported in the top half of the table.
locator: "Estimates of Home Purchases Attributable to the ARRA and WHBAA Homebuyer Tax Credits", Table 3
context: Congressional Research Service, 2010; ex ante simulation multiplying an assumed elasticity by the credit as a share of the median price; not an ex post causal estimate. Later causal studies (Berger, Turner and Zwick; Hembre) found larger effects.

statement: CRS estimated that after repayment the $7,500 HERA credit was worth only $2,104, or 1.0% of the price, and that falling prices and mortgage rates cut the typical buyer's payment about eight times as much as the ARRA credit did.

Combined, home prices and mortgages rates were estimated to be eight times more powerful at lowering the cost of homeownership than the tax credit.

statement: Berger, Turner and Zwick estimate the credit raised home sales by 490,000 (9.8%), raised median prices by $2,400 (1.1%) per standard deviation of program exposure, and raised the transition rate into homeownership by 53%; induced buyers were three years younger than typical first-time buyers (claimants' median age 32), and effects were concentrated in low-price ZIP codes.

statement: Across states and metros, Hembre finds the credit worked better where homes were cheaper (a doubling of average home values implies an effect 18.8 percentage points smaller) and finds a near-zero, insignificant coefficient on housing supply elasticity.

The supply elasticity coefficient is near zero and not statistically significant.
context: Regional Science and Urban Economics, 2018; peer-reviewed; local effects from Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and FHA loan data with the Saiz (2008) supply elasticity for selected metros; small samples.

statement: Dynan, Gayer and Plotkin conclude the federal and state homebuyer credits had at best small and mostly temporary effects on housing activity, with state programs giving less than a percentage point boost to prices and no rise in construction.
anchor: All told, our different analyses suggest that the various homebuyer tax credit programs had, at best, small and mostly temporary effects on housing activity.

the results suggest that any increase in demand did not translate into higher home construction activity
context: Brookings Institution working paper, June 2013; not peer-reviewed; national time series plus state-program panel; authors were Brookings Economic Studies co-directors (Gayer later a Treasury official under Bush; Dynan later Treasury under Obama).

statement: Brogaard and Roshak find no measurable rise in sales volume but prices in affected markets $6,116 higher during the credits, a gap that more than reversed ($6,470) after the final credit expired.

statement: Hilber and Turner find the mortgage interest deduction raises homeownership only for higher-income households in loosely regulated (elastic-supply) markets and lowers it in restrictive ones, at a subsidy cost of $28,397 per new homeowner per year.
anchor: We find that the MID boosts homeownership attainment only of higher income households in less tightly regulated housing markets. In more restrictive places an adverse effect exists.

context: Review of Economics and Statistics, 2014; peer-reviewed; PSID 1984-2007 with state-federal MID variation and the Saks regulation index for 83 metros; no stake identified.

statement: Using a Danish reform that cut the deduction for middle- and high-income households, Gruber, Jensen and Kleven find a precisely estimated zero effect on homeownership, but larger and more expensive homes, more debt and higher prices where the deduction was larger.

context: AEJ: Economic Policy, 2021; peer-reviewed; quasi-experiment from Denmark's 1987 tax reform using administrative data; external validity to the U.S. is a judgment.

statement: In Sommer and Sullivan's equilibrium model, eliminating the mortgage interest deduction lowers house prices, raises homeownership, cuts mortgage debt and improves welfare.
anchor: Eliminating the mortgage interest deduction causes house prices to decline, increases homeownership, decreases mortgage debt, and improves welfare.

context: American Economic Review, 2018; peer-reviewed; calibrated dynamic model (a simulation, not an observed outcome); first author a Federal Reserve Board economist.

statement: Glaeser and Shapiro argue the deduction is a poor tool for raising homeownership because it goes to the wealthy, who almost always own, and note the ownership rate stayed essentially constant from 1965 while the subsidy moved with inflation.

the ownership subsidy moves with inflation and has changed significantly between 1965 and today, but the homeownership rate has been essentially constant.

statement: A peer-reviewed study of a matched sample of 2005-2014 originations found state HFA borrowers about 30 percent less likely to default or foreclose than similar non-HFA borrowers, with 37 percent of the effect explained by HFA practices such as direct servicing and homeownership counseling.
anchor: Using a matched sample of HFA originations between 2005 and 2014, we estimate a multinomial logit model of mortgage default (or foreclosure) and prepayment.
We find that HFA borrowers are about 30 percent less likely to default or foreclose on their mortgages than otherwise similar non‐HFA borrowers.
We find that 37 percent of this HFA effect can be explained by HFA origination and service delivery practices including direct servicing and homeownership counseling.
context: Hembre, Moulton and Record, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management (2021). HFA loans usually come with DPA, so this compares a package (HFA first mortgage, DPA, counseling, servicing), not DPA alone.

statement: England's official evaluation of the Help to Buy equity loan put demand additionality, the share of buyers drawn in who could not otherwise have bought, at a central 37% once buyers who could have bought a smaller home are excluded; 79% of buyers said it let them buy sooner.
anchor: Demand additionality is defined as the extent to which the scheme has drawn in more buyers.
This results in a reduction in the central estimate from 41% to 37%.
Some 79% of buyers agreed it enabled them to buy a property sooner
context: Commissioned by the UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; buyer survey, not an experiment. The equity loan (20%, 40% in London) is the closest large analog to Dream For All. Implies roughly two in three assisted buyers would have bought anyway (project inference).

statement: Carozzi, Hilber and Yu found that Help to Buy significantly raised house prices with no detectable effect on construction in supply-constrained Greater London, while near the English/Welsh border it raised construction without a noticeable price effect.
anchor: we find that HtB significantly increased house prices and had no detectable effect on construction volumes in severely supply constrained and unaffordable Greater London.
HtB did increase construction numbers without a noticeable effect on prices near the English/Welsh border, an affordable area with comparably lax supply conditions.
context: Journal of Urban Economics (2024), peer-reviewed; difference-in-discontinuities. Capitalization depends on local supply elasticity.

statement: Krolage found that a 2018 Bavarian flat-rate home purchase subsidy raised single-family home prices in Bavarian border regions by approximately 10,000 euros more than across the border, consistent with full capitalization, with no effect on apartments.
anchor: in the second half of 2018, single-family home prices increased by roughly 10,000 euros more in Bavarian border regions than in neighboring regions of other states.

the prices of single-family homes increased by approximately 10,000 euros more in Bavarian border regions. This is consistent with a full capitalization of the subsidy. No effect is found for apartments, whose purchasers seldom qualify for the subsidy.
context: International Tax and Public Finance (2023), peer-reviewed; uses offer prices. A broad, untargeted grant to families; contrast the Irish Help to Buy grant, where Central Bank of Ireland researchers (McCann and Singh 2023, not entered) found buyers mostly kept the money as liquidity and only the highest-income buyers paid more.

statement: In a randomized experiment in Tulsa offering low-income renters matched savings for a down payment, the treatment group's homeownership gain through 2003 disappeared after the program ended because controls caught up quickly, suggesting the aid mainly changed the timing of purchases.
anchor: Prior work shows that, among households who rented in 1998, homeownership rates increased more through 2003 in the treatment group than for controls.
We show that control group renters caught up rapidly with the treatment group after the experiment ended.
Homeownership rates in the treatment group stayed flat until homeownership rates in the control group caught up.
context: Grinstein-Weiss et al., American Economic Journal: Economic Policy (2013); small sample, matched savings rather than a grant, and controls became eligible for other homebuyer aid after 2003.

statement: The Urban Institute's 2010 evaluation of seven shared-equity programs found very few owners lost homes to foreclosure, over 90 percent remained homeowners five years after purchase where data existed, and resellers' median returns ranged from 6.5 percent to 60.0 percent despite resale restrictions.
anchor: only a very small number of shared equity homeowners lose their home because of foreclosure; and a very high percentage of these low income, first-time homeowners (over 90 percent in the three programs for which data were available) remain homeowners five years after purchasing a shared equity home.
In all programs the median rate of return realized by resellers was at least 6.5 percent, and was as high as 60.0 percent (Table 8).
context: Temkin, Theodos and Price, Urban Institute, funded through NCB Capital Impact (Ford Foundation); seven selected programs, no comparison group of similar unassisted buyers. Returns are internal rates of return on small down payments.

statement: A 2011 survey of community land trusts found 1.30% of CLT homeowners' mortgages seriously delinquent at the end of 2010, versus 8.57% in the conventional market, although CLT owners are all low-to-moderate income.

Mortgages in the CLT sample are all held by low-to-moderate income homeowners, while mortgages in the conventional market are held by owners across all incomes.
context: Thaden, Lincoln Institute working paper commissioned by the National CLT Network (advocate); 62 CLTs, 3,143 mortgages; selection into CLTs and their underwriting are not separated from stewardship effects.

statement: When FHA cut its annual mortgage insurance premium by 50 basis points in January 2015 (from 135 to 85 basis points, about $1,000 less in the first year on a $200,000 loan), home purchase loans to the FHA-reliant population rose by nearly 14 percent; the response fell with income, with none among relatively high-income borrowers, and the authors found no evidence the cut raised house prices.

statement: The federal manufactured housing code preempts local building codes but not local zoning; courts largely uphold exclusions and conditional-use denials. A HUD-cited survey found the chance a HUD-code unit was placed fell from 77.5% to 53.9% where zoning was a significant barrier, and another survey found only 29 percent of communities treated manufactured and traditional housing comparably.
anchor: The Act does not preempt restrictive zoning, and Congress should amend the law to cover zoning restrictions.
Communities often require approval of manufactured housing as a conditional use, and approval as a conditional use is often denied.

In jurisdictions where zoning was rated as a significant barrier, the probability of units having been placed was significantly lower than in jurisdictions where zoning was rated as a minor barrier (dropping from 77.5% to 53.9%).
only 29 percent of communities had laws that treated traditional and manufactured housing comparably.
context: Law review article by Daniel Mandelker (Washington University School of Law), 2016; legal and case-law analysis, with survey figures quoted from a HUD regulatory-barriers study and a 1996 survey. Advocates amending federal law to preempt zoning barriers.

statement: Pew and the Center for Building in North America find single-stair buildings of four to six stories with small floor plates cost 6% to 13% less to build than dual-stair buildings, and the second stair and corridor take around 7% of floor area; all but three major U.S. cities (New York City, Seattle, Honolulu) require two stairs at that height. A Boston-area study it cites estimated 130,000 homes on vacant parcels near transit if the code changed.
anchor: Single-stairway four-to-six-story buildings with relatively small floor plates cost 6% to 13% less to construct than similar dual-stairway buildings.
The additional stairway and corridor consume around 7% of the building’s floor area.
Current U.S. building codes in all but three major cities (New York City, Seattle, and Honolulu) stipulate that apartment buildings four to six stories must have two stairways.
A study of the Boston area estimated that such a building code change had the potential to create 130,000 new homes simply by developing the vacant parcels within walking distance of transit.

context: Pew Charitable Trusts (nonpartisan, advocates single-stair reform) with the Center for Building in North America, 2025; contractor cost quotes and a fire-death analysis of New York City and Seattle buildings. The 130,000-home Boston figure is a secondary citation of another study, a capacity estimate rather than a forecast.

statement: Section 504 of the Housing Act of 1949 lets USDA make a repair loan, grant or both to an eligible very low-income applicant, leaves the maximum amounts to the Secretary, and sets no age limit.
anchor: The Secretary may make a loan, grant, or combined loan and grant to an eligible very low-income applicant in order to improve or modernize a rural dwelling, to make the dwelling safer or more sanitary, or to remove hazards.
The maximum amount of a grant, a loan, or a loan and grant shall not exceed such limitations as the Secretary determines to be appropriate.
context: Statute text, 2024 edition. 'No age limit' is this dossier's reading of the whole subsection: the age-62 rule for grants is in USDA's regulation, 7 CFR 3550.103(b) (EV-HOU-761). The ROAD to Housing Act later opened loans to low-income applicants (EV-HOU-762).

statement: USDA's own regulation, not the statute, limits Section 504 grants to applicants 62 or older; it also requires applicants to be unable to get help elsewhere, makes older families first use net assets above $20,000 and younger ones above $15,000, and makes grants repayable if the home is sold within 3 years.
anchor: ( b ) Age (grant only). To be eligible for grant assistance, an applicant must be 62 years of age or older at the time of application.

Applicants must be unable to obtain financial assistance at reasonable terms and conditions from non-RHS credit or grant sources and lack the personal resources to meet their needs. Elderly families must use any net family assets in excess of $20,000 to reduce their section 504 request. Non-elderly families must use any net family assets in excess of $15,000 to reduce their section 504 request.

Grant recipients are required to sign a repayment agreement which specifies that the full amount of the grant must be repaid if the property is sold in less than 3 years from the date the grant agreement was signed.
context: Regulation text as retrieved November 9, 2026. Read with the statute (EV-HOU-760): the age rule can be changed by rule.
